sections.body:
Acute heart failure is the rapid or gradual onset of HF symptoms and signs severe enough to need urgent treatment. **ESC 2026 renames it 'decompensated HF'** because many patients worsen over days rather than minutes, and some can be treated without admission.

This guide decides two things: **which precipitant needs specific treatment now** (CHAMPIT), and **which haemodynamic profile** (warm/cold, wet/dry) sets the initial therapy.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
Confirm HF, treat the trigger, then profile the patient at the bedside: perfusion first (warm or cold), congestion second (wet or dry).

[[figure:acute-heart-failure-algorithm]]

The four-box profile (Forrester haemodynamics, Stevenson bedside version) is the shared language of ESC and ACC/AHA; the drug choices follow from it.
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
**The four profiles**

| Profile | Congestion | Perfusion | Initial management |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warm-wet (commonest) | Yes | Adequate | IV loop diuretic; IV nitrate if SBP high (vascular type) |
| Cold-wet | Yes | Poor | SBP <90 or shock: inotrope +/- norepinephrine, then diuretic; SBP >=90: diuretic + cautious vasodilator, inotrope if no response |
| Cold-dry | No | Poor | Cautious fluid challenge, stop diuretics/vasodilators; inotrope if still hypoperfused |
| Warm-dry | No | Adequate | Compensated: optimise oral therapy, reconsider diagnosis |

**CHAMPIT precipitants (ESC 2021)**

| Letter | Cause | Specific action |
|---|---|---|
| C | Acute coronary syndrome | Immediate angiography (very high-risk ACS) |
| H | Hypertensive emergency | IV vasodilator + diuretic; pulmonary oedema: SBP <140 mmHg immediately (ESC) |
| A | Arrhythmia | Cardioversion / rate control / pacing |
| M | Mechanical cause (acute MR, VSR, rupture, valve thrombosis) | Echo, surgery or intervention, MCS bridge |
| P | Pulmonary embolism | Reperfusion if high risk |
| I | Infection | Antibiotics, source control |
| T | Tamponade | Pericardiocentesis |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
**Key numbers and classes**

| Item | Value / recommendation | Source |
|---|---|---|
| NP rule-out in acute HF | BNP <100 pg/mL, NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL, MR-proANP <120 pmol/L | ESC 2021 |
| IV loop diuretic for fluid overload | Recommended (class I, C) | ESC 2021 |
| Initial IV furosemide | 1-2x usual oral daily dose; 20-40 mg if diuretic-naive | ESC 2021 diuretic algorithm |
| Adequate early response | Urine Na typically >50-70 mmol/L at ~2 h and/or urine output >100-150 mL/h in first 6 h | ESC 2021 diuretic algorithm |
| Add acetazolamide or HCTZ in fluid overload | Should be considered (IIa, B1) | ESC 2026 |
| Urine Na-guided diuretic therapy | May be considered (IIb, B1) | ESC 2026 |
| IV vasodilator | May be considered when SBP >110 mmHg (IIb, B) | ESC 2021 |
| SGLT2i started in hospital after stabilisation | Recommended (I, B1) | ESC 2026 |
| Shock team for potential temporary MCS | Recommended (I, C) | ESC 2026 |
| Microaxial flow pump in selected STEMI-related cardiogenic shock (LV systolic dysfunction, no risk of hypoxic brain injury) | Should be considered (IIa, B1) | ESC 2026 |
| IABP in unselected cardiogenic shock | Not recommended (III, B1) | ESC 2026 |

ESC 2026 uses a new level-of-evidence scale (A, B1, B2, C).
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Acute HF vignettes always contain the bedside signs you need: the skin temperature, mental state and urine output tell you 'warm or cold'; the JVP, crackles and oedema tell you 'wet or dry'. Put the patient in a box and the first hour of treatment follows.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Cold is not the same as hypotensive.** A patient can be hypoperfused with a 'normal' BP (narrow pulse pressure, cold peripheries, oliguria, rising lactate).
- **Nitrates in the wrong patient:** avoid with SBP <90 mmHg, severe aortic stenosis and RV infarction (preload-dependent).
- **Diuretics in tamponade or cold-dry** worsen output.
- **Routine inotropes** in a warm or normotensive patient add arrhythmia and mortality risk without benefit.
- **Stopping all oral HF therapy on admission.** Continue foundational drugs unless shock, severe hypotension or hyperkalaemia; reduce beta-blocker in low-output states.
- **Morphine for pulmonary oedema** is not routine.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Elderly hypertensive woman, BP 190/110, sudden pink frothy sputum, warm peripheries -> warm-wet vascular type -> **IV nitrate + diuretic + NIV**.
- Cold clammy, confused, BP 80/50, rales, lactate 4 -> cardiogenic shock -> echo, ECG, inotrope/vasopressor, shock team; if STEMI -> emergency PCI.
- After 6 h of IV furosemide only 300 mL urine -> double the dose, then add acetazolamide or thiazide.
- Hypotension with clear lungs after aggressive diuresis -> cold-dry -> stop diuretic, careful fluid.
- New pansystolic murmur and pulmonary oedema 4 days after MI -> mechanical complication -> urgent echo and surgery.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Profile = **perfusion (warm/cold) x congestion (wet/dry)**; warm-wet is ~2/3 of admissions.
- Diuretic response is checked early (2 h urine sodium, 6 h urine output) and escalated quickly.
- ESC 2026: **'decompensated HF'** replaces 'acute HF'; in-hospital SGLT2i initiation is class I.
- Cardiogenic shock: treat the cause (revascularization for ACS), inotropes/vasopressors as bridge, selected MCS - not routine IABP.
- Decongest completely before discharge; start or continue foundational therapy before discharge and review within 1-2 weeks.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Decision guide: acute (decompensated) heart failure profiles

sections.body:
The baroreflex is the body's fast, moment-to-moment blood-pressure buffer. Stretch-sensitive receptors in the walls of the carotid sinus and aortic arch sense arterial pressure and feed it back to the brainstem, which adjusts vagal and sympathetic output to push pressure back toward its set point within seconds.

[[figure:baroreflex-loop]]
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
The loop:

1. Sensors: baroreceptors (stretch receptors) in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. They fire FASTER when the vessel wall is stretched more (higher pressure).
2. Afferents: carotid sinus -> glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX, via the nerve of Hering); aortic arch -> vagus (CN X). Both end in the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) of the medulla.
3. Integration: the NTS drives the cardiovascular centres in the medulla.
4. Efferents: vagal (parasympathetic) outflow to the SA/AV node and sympathetic outflow to heart and vessels.

When BP RISES: baroreceptor firing increases -> NTS -> vagal output UP and sympathetic output DOWN -> heart rate down, contractility down, venous tone down and systemic vascular resistance down -> BP falls back toward set point.

When BP FALLS: baroreceptors are unloaded (fire less) -> the brake comes off the sympathetic system and vagal output drops -> tachycardia, increased contractility and vasoconstriction -> BP rises back toward set point.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
- The baroreflex is a RAPID (seconds), NEGATIVE-feedback system — it buffers acute swings (e.g. standing up) but does NOT set long-term average pressure (the kidney/RAAS does that).
- It RESETS: in sustained hypertension the baroreceptors adapt to the higher pressure as the new 'normal', which is why they do not correct chronic hypertension.
- It is most sensitive around the normal operating pressure, where the stimulus–response curve is steepest.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: The baroreflex explains syncope, orthostatic hypotension, the HR response to vasoactive drugs, and why carotid sinus massage is a bedside tool for SVT. It is one of the most heavily tested physiology loops in the entrance exam.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Saying the baroreflex controls LONG-TERM blood pressure. It does not — it adapts/resets; long-term control is renal (pressure natriuresis / RAAS).
- Swapping the nerves: students often give the carotid sinus to the vagus. It is CN IX (glossopharyngeal); the aortic arch is the vagus (CN X).
- Getting the direction backwards: HIGHER pressure = MORE firing = a SLOWER heart (not faster).
- Forgetting that carotid sinus massage works by RAISING sensed pressure, which the brain answers with increased vagal tone.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- 'Neck pressure / tight collar / shaving causes syncope' -> carotid sinus hypersensitivity (an exaggerated baroreflex).
- 'BP drops and heart rate rises on standing' -> normal baroreflex response; if HR does NOT rise when BP falls, suspect autonomic failure or a chronotropic-blocking drug.
- 'A pressor drug (phenylephrine) is given and the heart rate falls' -> baroreflex bradycardia.
- 'Which afferent nerve carries carotid sinus signals?' -> glossopharyngeal (CN IX).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Carotid sinus -> CN IX (glossopharyngeal). Aortic arch -> CN X (vagus). Both -> NTS.
- High BP -> MORE baroreceptor firing -> vagal up / sympathetic down -> bradycardia + vasodilation.
- Low BP -> LESS firing -> reflex tachycardia + vasoconstriction.
- Carotid sinus massage raises local carotid pressure artificially -> reflex vagal surge -> slows AV conduction (diagnostic/therapeutic in regular narrow-complex SVT).
- Orthostasis: on standing, ~500–800 mL pools in the legs -> venous return and BP dip -> baroreceptors unload -> reflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction restore BP. A blunted reflex (autonomic neuropathy, hypovolaemia, certain drugs) causes orthostatic hypotension.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
The heart has its own pacemaker (the SA node) and will beat on its own, but moment-to-moment heart rate, conduction speed, force of contraction and speed of relaxation are set by the autonomic nervous system (ANS). Two opposing arms do this:

- Parasympathetic (vagus nerve, CN X) — releases acetylcholine (ACh) acting on M2 muscarinic receptors. Dominant at rest. Slows the heart.
- Sympathetic (cardiac sympathetic nerves from T1–T4 via the stellate/cervical ganglia) — releases noradrenaline (NA) acting mainly on beta-1 receptors. Dominant in stress/exercise. Speeds and strengthens the heart.

[[figure:ans-wiring]]
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
Wiring and targets:

- Right vagus -> mainly the SA node (so it chiefly controls RATE / chronotropy).
- Left vagus -> mainly the AV node (so it chiefly controls CONDUCTION / dromotropy).
- Parasympathetic fibres richly supply the SA node, AV node and atria, but only sparsely supply the ventricles — so vagal tone has a large effect on rate and AV conduction and only a small direct effect on ventricular force.
- Sympathetic fibres supply SA node, AV node, atrial AND ventricular myocardium, and the vessels — so sympathetic drive affects rate, conduction, force, relaxation and vascular tone.

Signalling:
- Sympathetic: NA -> beta-1 -> Gs -> adenylyl cyclase -> cAMP -> protein kinase A (PKA). PKA phosphorylates L-type Ca2+ channels (more Ca2+ in), phospholamban (faster SERCA Ca2+ reuptake), and the funny-current channels (faster phase-4 depolarisation).
- Parasympathetic: ACh -> M2 -> Gi -> LESS cAMP, and the Gi beta-gamma subunit opens acetylcholine-gated K+ channels (GIRK / I_KACh). The resulting K+ efflux hyperpolarises nodal cells and flattens the phase-4 slope, so the SA node fires less often and the AV node conducts more slowly.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
Four 'tropies' — know them cold:

- Chronotropy = heart rate (SA node firing). Sympathetic +, vagal -.
- Dromotropy = conduction velocity (mainly AV node). Sympathetic +, vagal -.
- Inotropy = force of contraction. Sympathetic ++ (ventricles); vagal effect on ventricles is small.
- Lusitropy = rate of relaxation (diastolic function). Sympathetic + (PKA phosphorylates phospholamban -> SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the SR faster -> faster, more complete relaxation).

Net effect: sympathetic activation raises cardiac output by increasing HR and stroke volume AND by shortening diastole without impairing filling (because relaxation speeds up). Vagal activation mainly drops heart rate and slows AV conduction.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Understanding this one page lets you predict the heart's response to drugs (beta-blockers, atropine, sympathomimetics, digoxin), to reflexes (baroreflex, carotid sinus massage) and to disease states (heart failure drives chronic sympathetic activation, which is why neurohormonal blockade with beta-blockers improves survival).
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- 'The vagus strongly weakens ventricular contraction' — FALSE. Vagal innervation of the ventricle is sparse; the big vagal effects are on RATE and AV CONDUCTION.
- Confusing lusitropy (relaxation) with inotropy (contraction). Beta-1 stimulation improves BOTH, which is why a faster, harder-beating heart can still fill in a shorter diastole.
- Thinking the resting heart has no autonomic input because it is 'automatic'. At rest the heart is under tonic vagal restraint.
- Mixing up which vagus does what: RIGHT vagus -> SA (rate); LEFT vagus -> AV (conduction).
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- A stem that says 'resting heart rate rose from 70 to ~100 after a drug' with no other change -> the drug is a muscarinic blocker (atropine) removing vagal tone.
- 'Carotid sinus massage terminated the tachycardia' -> a vagal manoeuvre increasing M2 drive to the AV node (negative dromotropy) — used in AVNRT/AVRT.
- 'Rate control in atrial fibrillation with a drug that also increases contractility' -> digoxin, whose main rate-slowing action is an INDIRECT vagotonic effect on the AV node.
- A question pairing a transmitter with a receptor: ACh–M2–Gi (slows heart); NA–beta1–Gs (speeds heart).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Resting heart rate (~60–80/min) is LOWER than the SA node's DENERVATED intrinsic firing rate (~100–110/min) because resting vagal tone acts as a constant brake. Give a healthy person atropine (blocks the vagus) and the rate climbs toward this intrinsic rate.
- Do not confuse that denervated rate with the ESCAPE-pacemaker hierarchy quoted on ECGs — the automaticity each tissue shows when it takes over: SA node 60–100/min; AV junction 40–60/min; His–Purkinje / ventricle 20–40/min.
- Neurotransmitters: sympathetic = noradrenaline (beta-1); parasympathetic = acetylcholine (M2). Preganglionic fibres of BOTH arms release ACh onto nicotinic ganglionic receptors.
- Vagal (parasympathetic) responses switch on and off FAST (ACh is broken down quickly by acetylcholinesterase); sympathetic responses are slower in onset and offset.
- The ventricle's force is governed far more by the sympathetic system and the Frank–Starling mechanism than by the vagus.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
Autonomic transmitters act through G-protein-coupled receptors. The receptor subtype AND the G-protein it couples to decide the downstream effect. Memorise the receptor -> G-protein -> second messenger -> tissue effect chain for the cardiovascular subtypes.

[[figure:adrenergic-cholinergic-receptors]]
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
Adrenergic (respond to noradrenaline/adrenaline):
- beta-1: heart (SA node, AV node, myocardium) and renal juxtaglomerular cells. Gs -> cAMP up. Effects: +chronotropy, +dromotropy, +inotropy, +lusitropy; renin release.
- beta-2: bronchial and vascular (esp. skeletal-muscle) smooth muscle; some in the heart. Gs -> cAMP up -> smooth-muscle RELAXATION (bronchodilation, vasodilation); adrenaline-sensitive.
- alpha-1: vascular smooth muscle. Gq -> phospholipase C -> IP3/DAG -> intracellular Ca2+ up -> VASOCONSTRICTION (raises SVR and venous tone).
- alpha-2: presynaptic nerve terminals and CNS. Gi -> cAMP down -> inhibits further NA release (negative feedback); central alpha-2 agonism (clonidine) lowers sympathetic outflow.

Cholinergic (respond to acetylcholine):
- M2 (muscarinic): SA and AV node (and atria). Gi -> cAMP down and opens K+ (GIRK/I_KACh) channels -> hyperpolarisation -> -chronotropy, -dromotropy.
- M3: vascular endothelium -> nitric oxide -> vasodilation (pharmacological/experimental; most vessels lack direct parasympathetic innervation).
- Nicotinic (N): autonomic ganglia and neuromuscular junction (ligand-gated ion channel, not GPCR).
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
Quick map of the Gs/Gi/Gq logic:

- Gs (beta-1, beta-2): cAMP UP. In heart = stimulate; in smooth muscle = relax.
- Gi (alpha-2, M2): cAMP DOWN. In heart = slow; presynaptically = less NA release.
- Gq (alpha-1): IP3/DAG/Ca2+ UP -> smooth-muscle contraction = vasoconstriction.

So the SAME catecholamine can raise the heart rate (beta-1), dilate muscle beds (beta-2) and constrict others (alpha-1) at once; the net blood-pressure effect depends on which receptors dominate at the dose given.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Nearly every cardiovascular drug in the exam works through one of these receptors. Knowing the receptor -> G-protein -> effect chain lets you reason out a drug's actions and side-effects instead of memorising lists.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Saying 'beta-2 stimulation speeds the heart'. beta-2's cardiovascular job is smooth-muscle RELAXATION (vasodilation/bronchodilation); cardiac acceleration is mainly beta-1.
- Pairing M2 with Gq or Gs. M2 is Gi (inhibitory, cAMP down).
- Pairing alpha-1 with cAMP. alpha-1 is Gq -> IP3/DAG, not the cAMP pathway.
- Forgetting that alpha-2 is largely PREsynaptic/central and INHIBITORY (clonidine lowers BP by reducing central sympathetic outflow, not by constricting vessels).
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- 'A drug lowers heart rate, contractility and renin release' -> beta-1 blocker.
- 'A centrally acting agent lowers blood pressure and can cause rebound hypertension if stopped abruptly' -> clonidine (alpha-2 agonist).
- 'Which receptor–G-protein pairing is correct?' -> beta1/Gs, alpha1/Gq, M2/Gi are the money answers.
- 'Inotrope of choice to augment contractility in cardiogenic shock without much vasoconstriction' -> dobutamine (beta-1 > beta-2).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- beta-1 = heart; beta-2 = lungs/vessels (relax). A neat memory: you have 1 heart and 2 lungs.
- beta-blockers (e.g. bisoprolol, metoprolol) blunt beta-1 -> lower HR, contractility and renin; cardioselective agents spare beta-2.
- beta-agonists: dobutamine (beta-1, inotrope); salbutamol (beta-2, bronchodilator). Isoprenaline is a non-selective beta-agonist.
- Atropine blocks M2 -> removes the vagal brake -> heart rate rises (treatment of symptomatic bradycardia).
- Phenylephrine (alpha-1 agonist) -> vasoconstriction -> raises BP and can trigger a reflex (baroreflex) bradycardia.
- Digoxin's main rate-slowing effect is INDIRECT: it increases vagal tone (M2 on the AV node). Its positive inotropy is separate (Na/K-ATPase inhibition -> more intracellular Ca2+).
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
Beyond the baroreflex, several named reflexes modulate heart rate and vascular tone. They are favourite one-liners in the exam — know the trigger and the response for each.

[[figure:cardiac-reflexes]]
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
- Bainbridge reflex (atrial stretch reflex): a rise in venous return stretches atrial receptors -> vagal afferents to the medulla -> net INCREASE in heart rate. It helps the heart keep up with incoming volume and is most influential when the starting heart rate is low.
- Bezold–Jarisch reflex: stimulation of cardiac chemo-/mechanoreceptors (unmyelinated C-fibres, mostly in the infero-posterior left ventricle) -> a vagally mediated TRIAD of bradycardia, hypotension and peripheral vasodilation (with apnoea). Classically seen in inferior STEMI/reperfusion, and it underlies much vasovagal syncope.
- Peripheral chemoreceptor reflex: carotid and aortic bodies sense low PaO2, high PaCO2 or low pH. The primary cardiac effect of hypoxia is bradycardia with sympathetic VASOCONSTRICTION; in the intact animal the accompanying hyperventilation (lung stretch) usually produces a secondary tachycardia.
- Cushing reflex: a dangerous rise in intracranial pressure causes brainstem ischaemia -> a massive sympathetic surge. The result is the CUSHING TRIAD: hypertension (wide pulse pressure), bradycardia (baroreflex response to the hypertension) and irregular/depressed respiration.
- Respiratory sinus arrhythmia: heart rate speeds up on inspiration and slows on expiration, driven by cyclical changes in vagal tone. It is a NORMAL sign of healthy vagal activity, most obvious in young, fit people.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
Trigger -> response at a glance:

- Bainbridge: venous return up -> HR up.
- Bezold–Jarisch: inferior-LV receptor stimulation -> bradycardia + hypotension + vasodilation.
- Chemoreceptor (hypoxia): O2 down / CO2 up -> bradycardia + vasoconstriction (primary), hyperventilation.
- Cushing: ICP up -> hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing.
- Respiratory sinus arrhythmia: inspiration -> vagal tone down -> HR up (and the reverse on expiration).
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: These reflexes turn confusing bedside pictures into one-line diagnoses: the hypotensive-bradycardic inferior MI, the brady-hypertensive head injury, the fainting blood-donor. They are compact, high-yield marks in the entrance exam.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Expecting a TACHYcardia in an inferior MI with the Bezold–Jarisch reflex. It causes BRADYcardia and hypotension.
- Reading respiratory sinus arrhythmia as pathological. It is normal.
- Calling the Cushing-reflex bradycardia a 'direct' effect of ICP. The bradycardia is the BAROREFLEX answering the sympathetically driven hypertension.
- Confusing Bainbridge (volume -> faster) with the baroreflex (pressure -> slower).
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- 'Inferior STEMI with bradycardia and hypotension' -> Bezold–Jarisch reflex (and/or RCA-supplied SA/AV nodal ischaemia).
- 'Head injury with rising BP, falling HR and irregular breathing' -> Cushing triad -> raised ICP.
- 'Rapid IV fluid or leg-raise increased the heart rate' -> Bainbridge reflex.
- 'Beat-to-beat HR variation with breathing in a healthy young athlete' -> respiratory sinus arrhythmia (reassure, no workup).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Bainbridge raises HR with volume loading; the baroreflex lowers HR with pressure loading. Which wins depends on the starting state — Bainbridge dominates at low heart rates, the baroreflex at high pressures.
- Bezold–Jarisch = bradycardia + hypotension; think INFERIOR MI (right coronary territory), reperfusion, and vasovagal faints.
- Cushing triad (hypertension + bradycardia + irregular respiration) signals raised intracranial pressure — a neuro-emergency, not a primary cardiac problem.
- Respiratory sinus arrhythmia is benign and a marker of good vagal tone; loss of beat-to-beat variability is a poor prognostic sign.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
**Acute aortic syndrome** = classic dissection, intramural haematoma (IMH), penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer (PAU) and rupture. This guide covers **who to image** (ADD-RS + D-dimer), **which test** (by stability), **what to do for A vs B**, and **how to control BP and heart rate** (beta-blocker first).

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
[[figure:aortic-dissection-algorithm]]

### ADD-RS (1 point per category, 0-3)
| Category | Features (any one scores the point) |
|---|---|
| High-risk conditions | Marfan or other connective tissue disease; family history of aortic disease; known aortic valve disease; recent aortic manipulation; known thoracic aortic aneurysm |
| High-risk pain features | Chest, back or abdominal pain that is abrupt in onset, severe, or ripping/tearing |
| High-risk examination features | Pulse deficit or systolic BP difference between limbs; focal neurological deficit with pain; new aortic regurgitation murmur with pain; hypotension or shock |

- ESC 2024: a multiparametric diagnostic algorithm using ADD-RS is recommended (**Class I**); ECG-gated contrast CT from neck to pelvis is the first-line imaging technique (**Class I**).
- Unstable patients: bedside TTE, then TOE (in theatre/ICU) or CT if they can be moved.
- A normal ECG and chest X-ray do **not** exclude dissection; ST elevation can mean coronary involvement (usually RCA).
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
### Classification and treatment
| Type | Definition | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Stanford A (DeBakey I, II) | Involves the ascending aorta, wherever the tear | Emergency surgery (Class I) |
| Stanford B (DeBakey IIIa/b) | Ascending aorta spared | Uncomplicated: medical (± subacute TEVAR, ESC 2024 IIa); complicated: TEVAR (ESC 2024 Class I) |
| Non-A non-B | Arch involved, ascending spared | Individualised (aortic team) |
| TEM (ESC 2024) | Type, Entry tear, Malperfusion | Adds entry site and malperfusion to plan treatment |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
### Anti-impulse therapy: ESC vs ACC/AHA
| Item | ESC 2014 | ACC/AHA 2022 |
|---|---|---|
| Heart rate | About 60 bpm or less | 60-80 bpm |
| Systolic BP | 100-120 mmHg | <120 mmHg, or lowest that keeps perfusion |
| First drug | IV beta-blocker (esmolol, labetalol, metoprolol) | IV beta-blocker |
| If beta-blocker contraindicated | Non-DHP CCB | Non-DHP CCB |
| Add if BP still high | Nitroprusside, nicardipine, nitroglycerin, urapidil | Vasodilator after rate control |
| Long term | Beta-blocker, BP control | Beta-blocker; imaging at 1, 6, 12 months then yearly |

- Pain relief with IV opioids.
- Type A: emergency surgery, do not wait for angiography.
- Complicated type B (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain/hypertension, expansion): TEVAR.
- Uncomplicated type B: medical therapy; subacute TEVAR should be considered (ESC 2024 IIa), particularly with high-risk features.
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Aortic dissection is the chest pain diagnosis where the wrong reflex (antithrombotics, vasodilator first, waiting for angiography) kills. The exam tests risk-based imaging, the A vs B split and the drug order.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Starting nitroprusside or nicardipine **before** a beta-blocker (reflex tachycardia, more shear).
- Giving thrombolysis/antiplatelets for 'STEMI' that is really dissection involving the RCA.
- Lowering BP in a **hypotensive** dissection (think tamponade, rupture, acute AR; pseudo-hypotension in a malperfused arm).
- Needle pericardiocentesis for tamponade in type A instead of surgery.
- Relying on D-dimer alone when ADD-RS is 2-3.
- Missing type A because CTPA (not an aortic protocol) was ordered.
- ESC and ACC/AHA targets differ: ESC HR ≤60 and SBP 100-120; ACC/AHA HR 60-80 and SBP <120.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Sudden tearing chest pain to the back, pulse or BP difference between arms, new early diastolic murmur -> **type A dissection**.
- Inferior STEMI + new AR murmur + wide mediastinum -> dissection involving the RCA: **do not lyse**.
- Marfan patient with chest pain -> ADD-RS at least 2 -> straight to CTA.
- Type B with abdominal pain and rising lactate -> **mesenteric malperfusion** = complicated -> TEVAR.
- 'First drug in acute dissection?' -> **IV beta-blocker** (esmolol/labetalol).
- Hypotension + muffled heart sounds + raised JVP in dissection -> **tamponade** -> surgery.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- ADD-RS 0-1 + D-dimer <500 ng/mL: AAS unlikely; ADD-RS 2-3: image directly.
- CTA first in stable patients; TTE/TOE when unstable.
- Type A = ascending involved = surgery; type B = medical unless complicated.
- Beta-blocker first; HR ~60, SBP 100-120 (ESC) / <120 (ACC/AHA).
- Follow-up imaging at 1, 6, 12 months then yearly.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Decision guide: suspected acute aortic dissection

sections.body:
This guide answers two exam questions: **is this AS truly severe?** (including the low-flow traps) and **does this patient need AVR now, and by which route?** ACC/AHA 2020 and ESC/EACTS 2021/2025 agree on the core triggers but differ on age cut-offs and on asymptomatic patients.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
[[figure:aortic-stenosis-algorithm]]

### Low-gradient severe AS (ACC/AHA stages D2 and D3)
| Pattern | LVEF | Flow | Next test | Severe if |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High-gradient (D1) | Any | Normal or any | None needed | Vmax ≥4 or MG ≥40 |
| Classical low-flow low-gradient (D2) | <50% | Low | Low-dose dobutamine echo | Vmax ≥4 / MG ≥40 with AVA ≤1.0 at any flow rate |
| Paradoxical low-flow low-gradient (D3) | ≥50% | SVi <35 mL/m² | CT calcium score (BP controlled) | Calcium above sex-specific threshold; AS judged the likely cause of symptoms |
| Normal-flow low-gradient | ≥50% | SVi ≥35 mL/m² | Recheck measurements | Usually moderate |
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
### Severity grading (echo)
| Parameter | Mild | Moderate | Severe |
|---|---|---|---|
| Peak velocity (Vmax) | 2.0-2.9 m/s | 3.0-3.9 m/s | ≥4.0 m/s (very severe ≥5) |
| Mean gradient | <20 mmHg | 20-39 mmHg | ≥40 mmHg (very severe ≥60) |
| Valve area (AVA) | >1.5 cm² | 1.0-1.5 cm² | <1.0 cm² (ACC/AHA ≤1.0) |
| Indexed AVA | - | - | <0.6 cm²/m² |
| Velocity ratio (DVI) | - | - | <0.25 |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
### Main AVR indications and classes
| Situation | ACC/AHA 2020 | ESC 2021 / 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Symptomatic severe high-gradient AS | 1 (A) | I |
| Asymptomatic severe AS, LVEF <50% | 1 (B-NR) | I (2021: I B) |
| Severe AS + other cardiac surgery | 1 | I |
| Symptomatic classical LFLG (D2) | 1 | I, after careful confirmation of severity (DSE or CT calcium) |
| Symptomatic paradoxical LFLG (D3) | 1 if AS is the likely cause | IIa (after careful confirmation) |
| Asymptomatic, abnormal exercise test | 2a (BP fall) / 1 (symptoms) | I (symptoms); IIa (BP fall >20 mmHg) |
| Asymptomatic, Vmax ≥5, BNP >3x normal or rapid progression, low risk | 2a | IIa (2021: Vmax >5 m/s, calcification + progression, BNP >3x; LVEF <55% also IIa) |
| Asymptomatic severe AS, LVEF ≥50%, low risk (early AVR) | - | ESC 2025: IIa (A) |
| TAVI vs SAVR by age | <65 SAVR; 65-80 shared; >80 TAVI | ESC 2025: ≥70 TAVI (I A); <70 low risk SAVR (I) |

- Decide through a **Heart Team** in a heart valve centre.
- Symptoms + severe AS = intervene (no medical therapy changes survival).
- Exercise testing unmasks symptoms in sedentary patients but is **contraindicated in symptomatic** severe AS.
- Bicuspid valves, young age and need for other cardiac surgery favour SAVR.
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: AS is the commonest valve lesion needing intervention in older adults, and the PPDS exam loves its discordant-grading puzzles. Recognising true severe AS behind a low gradient, and knowing when TAVI or surgery is the right answer, are the decisions a cardiology resident makes every week.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Trusting a low gradient in a patient with **low flow** (LVEF <50% or SVi <35): the AS may still be severe.
- An AVA error from the **LVOT diameter** (it is squared in the continuity equation).
- Calling 'asymptomatic' a patient who has simply reduced activity: do an exercise test.
- Exercise testing a **symptomatic** severe AS patient.
- Vasodilators/nitrates and aggressive diuresis in severe AS (preload-dependent, fixed obstruction).
- Remembering only ESC 2021 (75 y) for TAVI: **ESC 2025 lowered it to 70 y**; ACC/AHA 2020 uses 65 and 80.
- Statins do not slow AS progression.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Elderly man, syncope on exertion, slow-rising pulse, soft or single S2, ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids -> severe AS.
- Murmur peaking late and a soft A2 = more severe; the murmur can become **quieter** as the LV fails.
- LVEF 30%, MG 25 mmHg, AVA 0.8 cm² -> **dobutamine stress echo**.
- Small hypertrophied LV, LVEF 65%, SVi 30 mL/m², MG 30 mmHg, AVA 0.8 cm² -> **paradoxical LFLG** -> CT calcium score.
- Angina + syncope + dyspnoea: classic survival without AVR roughly 5, 3 and 2 years.
- Heyde syndrome: AS + GI angiodysplasia bleeding (acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Severe AS: **Vmax ≥4 m/s, MG ≥40 mmHg, AVA <1.0 cm²** (indexed <0.6).
- Flow reserve on DSE = SV increase ≥20%.
- Paradoxical LFLG: LVEF ≥50%, SVi <35 mL/m².
- Class I triggers: symptoms; LVEF <50%; concomitant cardiac surgery.
- ESC 2025: TAVI ≥70 y (I A), SAVR <70 y low risk; early intervention in asymptomatic severe AS with LVEF ≥50% is IIa.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Decision guide: aortic stenosis (severity and intervention)

sections.body:
Arrhythmias arise from **abnormal impulse formation**, **abnormal impulse conduction**, or both.
- **Impulse formation:** **automaticity** (enhanced normal or abnormal) and **triggered activity** (early or delayed afterdepolarisations).
- **Impulse conduction:** **block** (bradyarrhythmias, and the unidirectional block that starts re-entry) and **re-entry**, the commonest mechanism of clinically important tachycardias.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
### 1. Automaticity
**Enhanced normal automaticity** - cells that already pace (SA node, AV junction, Purkinje fibres) depolarise faster in phase 4 because the **funny current (If)** and Ca2+ currents increase: sympathetic tone, fever, hypovolaemia, thyrotoxicosis. Examples: sinus tachycardia, accelerated junctional rhythm. Normal pacemakers are **overdrive-suppressed** by a faster rhythm (the Na+/K+ pump hyperpolarises them), which is why the SA node normally keeps control.

**Abnormal automaticity** - **working myocytes** that are partly depolarised (ischaemia, stretch, electrolyte disturbance) start firing spontaneously although they have no pacemaker function normally. It is **little affected by overdrive**. Examples usually attributed to it: some focal atrial tachycardias, accelerated idioventricular rhythm after reperfusion, early ischaemic ventricular ectopy.

Clues to an automatic rhythm: **gradual warm-up and cool-down**, cannot be started or stopped by programmed premature beats, and **DC cardioversion does not stop it** (the focus simply fires again).

### 2. Triggered activity
An **afterdepolarisation** is an oscillation of membrane potential that follows an action potential; if it reaches threshold it **triggers** a new beat, and one beat can trigger the next.

[[figure:afterdepolarisations]]

**Early afterdepolarisations (EADs)** - during **phase 2 or 3** of a **prolonged** action potential. When repolarising K+ current is reduced (IKr block, congenital long QT) or late Na+ current is increased, the plateau lasts long enough for **L-type Ca2+ channels to reactivate**. EADs are **bradycardia- and pause-dependent** (APD is longest at slow rates), typically start after a **short-long-short** sequence and cause **torsades de pointes**. Aggravated by hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia and QT-prolonging drugs.

**Delayed afterdepolarisations (DADs)** - **after** full repolarisation (**phase 4**). **SR Ca2+ overload** causes spontaneous Ca2+ release through RyR2; the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger removes that Ca2+ by bringing in 3 Na+ for each Ca2+, a net **inward current** that depolarises the cell. DADs are **tachycardia- and catecholamine-dependent** (faster rates load more Ca2+). Causes: **digoxin toxicity** (Na+/K+-ATPase block -> more intracellular Na+ -> less Ca2+ extrusion), catecholamines, **CPVT** (RyR2 or calsequestrin mutations), ischaemia-reperfusion; **RVOT VT** is cAMP-mediated triggered activity.

### 3. Re-entry
An impulse travels round a circuit and **re-excites tissue it has already activated**. Three requirements:
1. **Two pathways** joined at both ends around a central obstacle (anatomical, such as the tricuspid annulus or a scar, or functional).
2. **Unidirectional block** in one pathway (usually because it is still refractory to a premature beat).
3. **Conduction slow enough** in the other pathway that the blocked pathway has recovered by the time the impulse returns, so it can be entered retrogradely.

[[figure:reentry-circuit]]

The **wavelength** (conduction velocity x effective refractory period) must be **shorter than the circuit** so that an **excitable gap** of recovered tissue always lies ahead of the wavefront. Anything that **slows conduction or shortens refractoriness** shortens the wavelength and favours re-entry; **prolonging refractoriness** lengthens it and can stop re-entry.

Clinical re-entry: **AVNRT** (slow and fast AV nodal pathways), **AVRT** (accessory pathway; orthodromic = down the AV node, up the pathway: narrow QRS), **typical atrial flutter** (round the tricuspid annulus through the cavotricuspid isthmus), **scar-related VT** after MI, bundle-branch re-entry. **AF and VF** are maintained by multiple wavelets and rotors (functional re-entry). Re-entry is **started and stopped by premature beats**, can be **entrained** by pacing and is **terminated by DC cardioversion**.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
**ECG signatures that point to a mechanism:**
- **Warm-up / cool-down, variable rate:** automatic (sinus tachycardia, focal AT, accelerated idioventricular rhythm).
- **Abrupt start with a premature beat and abrupt stop:** re-entry (AVNRT, AVRT, flutter).
- **Pause-dependent onset, long QT, twisting QRS axis:** EAD-triggered **torsades de pointes**.
- **Bidirectional VT** (beat-to-beat alternating QRS axis): DAD-triggered - **digoxin toxicity** or **CPVT**.
- **Atrial tachycardia with AV block:** classic digoxin toxicity (DADs plus vagal AV slowing).
- **LBBB-like VT with an inferior axis, adenosine-sensitive:** RVOT VT (cAMP-mediated triggered activity).
- **Sawtooth flutter waves at about 300/min with 2:1 block (ventricular rate ~150):** macro-re-entry round the tricuspid annulus.
sections.title: ECG

sections.body:
### Matching the drug to the mechanism

| Drug class (Vaughan Williams) | Main action | Electrophysiological effect | Mechanism it targets | Examples and notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| IA | Na+ block (intermediate) + K+ block | Slower conduction (wider QRS) and longer APD/ERP (longer QT) | Re-entry (longer ERP, depressed conduction) | Procainamide (pre-excited AF), quinidine (Brugada, via Ito block); can cause EAD/torsades |
| IB | Na+ block, fast on-off, prefers depolarised tissue | Little effect on normal tissue; suppresses ischaemic, partly depolarised myocardium; shortens APD | Abnormal automaticity and re-entry in **ischaemic ventricle**; late Na+ current | Lidocaine (VT in ischaemia), mexiletine (LQT3) |
| IC | Na+ block, slow off (strong use-dependence) | Marked conduction slowing (QRS widens at fast rates) | Re-entry (AF, AVRT); DADs in CPVT (flecainide also blocks RyR2) | Flecainide, propafenone; **avoid in structural/ischaemic heart disease (CAST)** |
| II | Beta-blockade | Flatter phase 4 slope, slower AV node, less Ca2+ loading | Enhanced automaticity, catecholamine DADs (CPVT, RVOT VT), AV-node re-entry, LQT1/LQT2 | Bisoprolol, metoprolol, propranolol, nadolol |
| III | K+ (IKr) block | Longer APD and ERP (longer QT) | **Re-entry** (longer wavelength, smaller excitable gap) | Amiodarone (multi-channel, low torsades risk), sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide; others can cause EAD/torsades |
| IV | L-type Ca2+ block (non-DHP) | Slower AV node conduction, longer AV nodal ERP | AV-node-dependent re-entry; rate control; some DAD/Ca2+-dependent VT | Verapamil, diltiazem (idiopathic fascicular VT and RVOT VT respond) |
| Others | Adenosine (A1: K+ channel opening, less cAMP); magnesium; ivabradine (If block); digoxin (vagal) | Transient AV block; EAD suppression; slower SA node | AVNRT/AVRT termination and RVOT VT (adenosine); torsades (Mg2+); sinus node automaticity (ivabradine) | Adenosine also unmasks flutter/AT by blocking the AV node |

**Mechanism-specific rules:**
- **Torsades (EAD):** IV **magnesium**, correct K+, stop QT-prolonging drugs, **raise the heart rate** (isoprenaline or pacing) to shorten the APD.
- **Digoxin toxicity (DAD):** digoxin-specific antibody fragments; correct K+; avoid DC cardioversion if possible.
- **CPVT:** beta-blocker (nadolol), add flecainide; avoid catecholamines.
- **Re-entry:** break the circuit at its weakest link: **adenosine or vagal manoeuvres** for AV-node-dependent SVT, ablation of the slow pathway, accessory pathway or cavotricuspid isthmus, class III/IC drugs.
- **Automatic tachycardias** respond to rate slowing and treatment of the cause, **not to cardioversion**.
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Treatment follows mechanism. Re-entry is cured by breaking the circuit, automatic rhythms by removing the drive, EADs by shortening repolarisation and DADs by unloading calcium. Recognising the mechanism from the clinical setting and ECG tells you why magnesium works in torsades, why cardioversion fails in automatic tachycardia and why AV-nodal blockers can kill in pre-excited AF.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Torsades is pause- and bradycardia-dependent**: speeding the heart up is treatment, and beta-blockers given at the time can make acquired torsades worse.
- **Digoxin toxicity is worsened by hypokalaemia** (less competition at the Na+/K+-ATPase), yet very high K+ is also a sign of severe toxicity.
- **Class IC drugs in atrial flutter** can slow the flutter rate enough to allow **1:1 AV conduction** with a wide QRS; give an AV-nodal blocker with them.
- **AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, beta-blockers, digoxin) are dangerous in pre-excited AF**: they favour conduction down the accessory pathway; use procainamide or ibutilide, or cardiovert.
- Amiodarone prolongs QT but **rarely** causes torsades (homogeneous APD prolongation and Ca2+ block).
- **Lidocaine** has little effect on atrial arrhythmias (short atrial APD, few inactivated channels).
- A tachycardia that keeps recurring immediately after successful cardioversion is probably **automatic**, not re-entrant.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Long QT, hypokalaemia, pause, then polymorphic VT with twisting axis" -> **EAD -> torsades; IV magnesium**.
- "Elderly on digoxin, nausea, yellow vision, bidirectional VT" -> **DAD (Ca2+ overload) -> digoxin Fab**.
- "Child with exercise-induced syncope, normal resting ECG, bidirectional VT on exercise test" -> **CPVT (RyR2), beta-blocker +/- flecainide**.
- "Narrow-complex tachycardia that starts and stops abruptly and is terminated by adenosine" -> **AV-node-dependent re-entry (AVNRT/AVRT)**.
- "Which requirement of re-entry does class III therapy attack?" -> **lengthens the ERP, so the wavelength exceeds the circuit (no excitable gap)**.
- "LBBB morphology, inferior axis VT in a structurally normal heart, terminated by adenosine" -> **RVOT VT (triggered activity)**.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Automaticity**: enhanced normal (If, sympathetic) vs abnormal (partly depolarised myocytes); warm-up, not cardiovertible.
- **EAD = phase 2-3, long APD, bradycardia/pause-dependent, L-type Ca2+ reactivation -> torsades. Treat with Mg2+ and faster heart rate.**
- **DAD = phase 4, SR Ca2+ overload, NCX inward current, tachycardia/catecholamine-dependent -> digoxin toxicity, CPVT, RVOT VT, bidirectional VT.**
- **Re-entry needs two pathways, unidirectional block and slow conduction**; wavelength = CV x ERP must be shorter than the circuit.
- **Class III lengthens ERP (anti-re-entry); class IC slows conduction; class IB targets ischaemic tissue; class II and IV act on Ca2+-dependent nodal and triggered activity.**
- **Adenosine terminates AV-node-dependent re-entry and cAMP-triggered RVOT VT**, not flutter, AF or most scar VT.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
AF management is a series of separate decisions, not one. ESC 2024 organises them as **AF-CARE**: **C** comorbidity and risk-factor management, **A** avoid stroke and thromboembolism, **R** reduce symptoms by rate and rhythm control, **E** evaluation and dynamic reassessment. Before any of that: is the patient unstable, and is it pre-excited AF?

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
Pick the step you are deciding. Anticoagulation is decided by stroke risk, **not** by whether you choose rate or rhythm control.

[[figure:atrial-fibrillation-algorithm]]
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
**Stroke risk scores**

| Item | CHA2DS2-VA (ESC 2024) | CHA2DS2-VASc (ACC/AHA 2023) |
|---|---|---|
| Congestive HF / LV dysfunction | 1 | 1 |
| Hypertension | 1 | 1 |
| Age >=75 | 2 | 2 |
| Diabetes | 1 | 1 |
| Stroke / TIA / thromboembolism | 2 | 2 |
| Vascular disease | 1 | 1 |
| Age 65-74 | 1 | 1 |
| Female sex | - (removed) | 1 |

**Anticoagulation thresholds**

| Risk | ESC 2024 | ACC/AHA 2023 |
|---|---|---|
| High | CHA2DS2-VA >=2: OAC recommended | Annual risk >=2% (CHA2DS2-VASc >=2 men, >=3 women): COR 1 |
| Intermediate | CHA2DS2-VA 1: OAC should be considered | 1-2%/year (1 men, 2 women): reasonable |
| Low | 0: no OAC | 0 men, 1 women: no OAC |
| Mechanical valve or moderate-severe MS | VKA (no DOAC) | VKA (no DOAC) |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
**ESC 2024 vs ACC/AHA 2023: differences worth memorising**

| Topic | ESC 2024 | ACC/AHA 2023 |
|---|---|---|
| Framework | AF-CARE | AF stages 1-4 (at risk, pre-AF, AF 3A-3D, permanent) |
| Score | CHA2DS2-VA | CHA2DS2-VASc or other validated score; threshold by annual risk |
| Cardioversion without prior OAC/TOE | AF <24 h | AF <48 h |
| Wait-and-see for recent-onset AF | Should be considered | - |
| Catheter ablation first-line | Option in symptomatic paroxysmal AF | Useful in selected younger patients with paroxysmal AF |
| AF with HFrEF | Ablation in selected (e.g., suspected tachycardia cardiomyopathy) | Ablation recommended in appropriate patients |
| LAAO when OAC contraindicated | May be considered (IIb) | Reasonable (COR 2a) |

**Rate-control drugs by LVEF**

| LVEF | Options | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| >40% | Beta-blocker, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin | - |
| <=40% | Beta-blocker and/or digoxin (amiodarone acutely) | Diltiazem, verapamil |

Lenient initial target: resting HR typically <110 bpm.
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: AF is the most common sustained arrhythmia and an exam favourite because each decision has a clean rule. Separate the questions - instability, stroke, symptoms - and most vignettes answer themselves.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Rhythm control means no anticoagulation** - wrong: OAC follows the stroke score, not the rhythm.
- **DOAC in rheumatic mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve** - wrong: VKA (INVICTUS, RE-ALIGN).
- **Aspirin as a 'safer' alternative** - it is not effective stroke prevention in AF.
- **AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF** (adenosine, verapamil, digoxin, beta-blocker, IV amiodarone) can trigger VF.
- **Diltiazem/verapamil with LVEF <=40%.**
- **Withholding OAC because of a high bleeding score** - treat modifiable bleeding risks instead.
- **Cardioverting a 30-h episode without OAC/TOE** under ESC 2024 (cut-off now 24 h).
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- 70-year-old hypertensive woman: CHA2DS2-VA = 2 (age 65-74 + HTN) -> DOAC. Under CHA2DS2-VASc she scores 3.
- AF with rheumatic MS (MVA 1.2 cm2) -> **warfarin**, regardless of score.
- AF at 180 bpm, BP 70/40, confused -> synchronized cardioversion now.
- Irregular broad complexes at 260 bpm in a young man -> pre-excited AF -> procainamide or DC cardioversion; never verapamil.
- HFrEF with persistent AF and rising LVEF after rate control fails -> consider ablation.
- New AF, onset 10 h ago, stable -> rate control and wait-and-see, or early cardioversion with anticoagulation.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **AF-CARE** (ESC 2024) replaces ABC.
- **CHA2DS2-VA** drops female sex; thresholds 2 (recommended) and 1 (should be considered).
- **DOAC preferred** over VKA except mechanical valves and moderate-severe MS.
- **Cardioversion safety window:** ESC 24 h, ACC/AHA 48 h; otherwise 3 weeks OAC or TOE, and OAC >=4 weeks after.
- Unstable AF: synchronized cardioversion; AHA 2025: an initial energy of at least 200 J is reasonable for AF (2a, B-R).
- Early rhythm control (within 12 months of diagnosis) improved outcomes in EAST-AFNET 4.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
This guide decides two things for a slow heart rate: **what to do now** (atropine, pacing, chronotropes) if the patient is unstable, and **whether a permanent pacemaker is needed**, which depends on the rhythm (sinus node vs AV node vs infra-Hisian), symptoms, and reversible causes.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
First stability, then rhythm. In sinus node disease, symptoms decide. In Mobitz II, high-grade or complete AV block that is not reversible, the block itself decides - pace regardless of symptoms.

[[figure:bradycardia-av-block-algorithm]]
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
**AV block: level and pacing**

| Block | Usual level | QRS / escape | Atropine | Permanent pacing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| First-degree (PR >200 ms) | AV node | Narrow | Responds | Only if symptoms clearly attributable (marked PR prolongation) |
| Mobitz I (Wenckebach) | AV node | Narrow | Responds | Only if symptomatic or infra-Hisian |
| Mobitz II | His-Purkinje | Often wide | Often no effect | Yes, regardless of symptoms (if not reversible) |
| 2:1 | Either | Narrow suggests node, wide suggests infra-His | Variable | Decide by level and symptoms |
| High-grade / third-degree | Node (narrow escape 40-60) or infra-His (wide escape 20-40) | Variable | Node-level may respond | Yes, regardless of symptoms (if not reversible) |
| Alternating BBB | Infra-His | Wide | - | Yes, with or without symptoms (ESC 2021) |
| Bifascicular block + syncope | Infra-His | Wide | - | If HV >=70 ms or induced infra-His block (ESC 2021) |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
**Acute drugs and devices**

| Step | Dose / detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Atropine | 1 mg IV every 3-5 min, maximum 3 mg | AHA ACLS (2020 change from 0.5 mg; carried into 2025 materials) |
| Dopamine | 5-20 mcg/kg/min | AHA ACLS |
| Epinephrine | 2-10 mcg/min | AHA ACLS |
| Transcutaneous pacing | Bridge; confirm mechanical capture | ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 (may be considered) |
| Temporary transvenous pacing | Persistent unstable bradycardia refractory to drugs | ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 (reasonable) |
| Permanent pacing, acquired Mobitz II / high-grade / CHB not reversible | Regardless of symptoms | ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 COR 1; ESC 2021 indicated |
| CRT or His-bundle pacing instead of RV pacing | LVEF 36-50% with expected ventricular pacing >40% | ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 (reasonable) |

**Reversible causes to check first:** beta-blocker, non-DHP CCB, digoxin, antiarrhythmics, hyperkalaemia, acute inferior MI, hypothyroidism, hypothermia, sleep apnoea, Lyme carditis, raised intracranial pressure.
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Bradycardia questions hinge on locating the block. Once you know whether it is the sinus node, the AV node, or the His-Purkinje system, the acute drug response and the pacing indication follow logically.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Relying on atropine in Mobitz II or wide-escape complete block** - the block is below the node; go to pacing.
- **Atropine after heart transplant** - denervated heart, may cause paradoxical block; use pacing or catecholamines.
- **Pacing asymptomatic sinus bradycardia, sleep pauses or athletes** - not indicated.
- **Not pacing asymptomatic complete heart block** - acquired, non-reversible CHB or Mobitz II needs a pacemaker regardless of symptoms.
- **Calling drug-associated AV block 'reversible'** too quickly - it often unmasks intrinsic disease.
- **Electrical capture without a pulse** on transcutaneous pacing.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Inferior STEMI with complete heart block, narrow escape at 50 bpm -> AV-nodal, often transient; revascularize, atropine, temporary pacing if unstable.
- Anterior STEMI with new RBBB and Mobitz II -> infra-Hisian, high risk -> temporary pacing.
- Asymptomatic 70-year-old with incidental complete heart block, wide escape 35 bpm -> permanent pacemaker.
- Fit 25-year-old runner with HR 42 and Mobitz I at night -> reassurance.
- AF with a regular ventricular rate of 40 on digoxin -> complete heart block / digoxin toxicity.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Unstable bradycardia:** atropine 1 mg (max 3 mg) -> pacing or dopamine/epinephrine.
- **Narrow QRS block is usually nodal and benign; wide QRS block is infra-Hisian and dangerous.**
- **SND:** symptoms decide (no rate threshold); **acquired Mobitz II/high-grade/CHB:** pace regardless of symptoms.
- Minimise RV pacing in reduced LVEF: CRT or conduction-system pacing.
- After inferior MI, many AV blocks recover - observe before a permanent device (ESC 2021: wait at least 5 days).
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Decision guide: bradycardia and AV block

sections.body:
This guide follows the 2025 AHA adult cardiac arrest algorithm: **shockable or not**, what goes in every 2-minute cycle, when each drug is due, which reversible cause to hunt, and what to do after ROSC. ERC differences in drug timing are flagged.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
[[figure:cardiac-arrest-algorithm]]

**CPR quality**: rate 100-120/min; depth at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm; full recoil; pauses under 10 s; 30:2 until an advanced airway, then 1 breath every 6 s with continuous compressions; avoid over-ventilation; change compressor every 2 min; single shocks (not stacked), CPR resumed immediately after each shock. Vascular access: **IV first** (AHA 2025 COR 1, A), IO if IV fails (2a A).
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
### Arrest drugs and timing
| Drug | Dose | When (AHA) | Class (AHA 2025) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adrenaline (epinephrine) | 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 min | Non-shockable: as soon as feasible. Shockable: after initial shocks fail (usually after shock 2) | 2a B-R (dose); 2a B-NR (timing) |
| Amiodarone | 300 mg bolus, then 150 mg | Persisting VF/pVT (after shock 3) | 2b B-R (amiodarone or lidocaine) |
| Lidocaine | 1-1.5 mg/kg, then 0.5-0.75 mg/kg | Alternative to amiodarone | 2b B-R |
| Vasopressin | - | Do not substitute for adrenaline | 3: No Benefit |
| High-dose adrenaline | - | Not routine | 3: No Benefit |
| Calcium, bicarbonate, magnesium | - | Not routine; only for specific causes (hyperkalaemia, toxins, torsades) | 3: No Benefit (routine use) |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
### Post-ROSC targets (AHA 2025)
| Item | Target | Class |
|---|---|---|
| Mean arterial pressure | ≥65 mmHg | 1, B-R |
| Oxygen | 100% until reliable SpO2, then SpO2 90-98% (PaO2 60-105) | 1 / 2a, B-R |
| PaCO2 | 35-45 mmHg | 1, B-R |
| Temperature (not following commands) | 32-37.5 °C | 1, B-R |
| Duration of temperature control | At least 36 h | 2a, B-R |
| Coronary angiography: ST elevation | Emergent | 1, B-NR |
| Coronary angiography: no STE, stable | Not emergent | 3: No Benefit, B-R |
| Prognostication | Multimodal, ≥72 h after normothermia | 2a, B-NR |

**H's and T's**: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo-/hyperkalaemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis (pulmonary), thrombosis (coronary).
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Every cardiology resident leads resuscitations from the first week. The exam tests the sequence and the timing rather than rare facts, and post-ROSC care (angiography, temperature, targets) is where cardiologists make the decisions that change neurological outcome.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Giving adrenaline **before the first shock** in VF: defibrillation comes first; adrenaline after initial shocks fail.
- Delaying adrenaline in asystole/PEA (give it as soon as feasible).
- Stacked shocks or long pauses for pulse checks.
- Atropine in asystole/PEA (removed from the arrest algorithm since 2010).
- Routine calcium, bicarbonate or magnesium (no benefit; reserve for specific causes).
- Emergency angiography for every comatose survivor without ST elevation (no benefit if stable).
- Prognosticating on day 1: wait at least 72 h after normothermia, off sedation, multimodal.
- Using ETCO2 alone to stop resuscitation.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- 'Drug after the 2nd shock in VF?' -> **adrenaline 1 mg** (AHA). 'After the 3rd shock?' -> **amiodarone 300 mg**.
- ERC: both adrenaline and amiodarone after the **3rd** shock.
- Arrest in a dialysis patient with peaked T waves -> **calcium** + treat hyperkalaemia.
- PEA arrest after a long flight, dilated RV on POCUS -> **thrombolysis** for PE.
- Sudden ETCO2 jump from 15 to 40 mmHg during CPR -> **ROSC**.
- Comatose after ROSC: temperature control 32-37.5 °C for ≥36 h; MAP ≥65.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Shockable: shock -> CPR 2 min -> repeat; adrenaline after shock 2, amiodarone after shock 3 (AHA).
- Non-shockable: adrenaline ASAP, every 3-5 min.
- Amiodarone 300 then 150; lidocaine 1-1.5 then 0.5-0.75 mg/kg.
- DSED/vector change: not established (2b).
- Post-ROSC: MAP ≥65; SpO2 90-98%; PaCO2 35-45; 32-37.5 °C ≥36 h; prognosis ≥72 h.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Decision guide: adult cardiac arrest and post-ROSC care

sections.body:
**Cardiogenic shock** is a cardiac disorder causing clinical and biochemical evidence of sustained tissue hypoperfusion; hypotension is usual but not required (normotensive shock). This guide stages severity (SCAI), finds the cause, and picks the right reperfusion, device and drug.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
[[figure:cardiogenic-shock-algorithm]]

- Every suspected shock: **ECG, lactate, bedside echo** within minutes.
- Phenotype (PA catheter if available): LV-dominant (PCWP >15), RV-dominant (RA/CVP >15 with normal PCWP; RA:PCWP >0.6), or biventricular.
- Cardiac power output and PAPi (AMI-CS: <0.9) help choose and escalate support.
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
### SCAI SHOCK stages (2019, updated 2022)
| Stage | Description | Typical findings |
|---|---|---|
| A - At risk | No shock yet | Normal JVP, warm, lactate normal, SBP ≥100 or baseline |
| B - Beginning | Instability without hypoperfusion | SBP <90, MAP <60 or drop >30 mmHg, or HR ≥100; lactate normal; perfusion intact |
| C - Classic | Hypoperfusion needing one intervention beyond fluids | Cold/clammy, oliguria, confusion; lactate ≥2; CI <2.2, PCWP >15 |
| D - Deteriorating | Like C but worsening despite initial therapy | Rising lactate, worsening organ function, escalating drugs or MCS |
| E - Extremis | Circulatory collapse | Ongoing CPR/ECMO; lactate ≥8, pH <7.2, base deficit >10 |
| Modifier 'A' | Cardiac arrest with coma | GCS <9 after arrest; worse prognosis at any stage |
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
- **Emergency culprit revascularisation** (PCI or CABG) in ACS-CS irrespective of time from onset: ACC/AHA 2025 COR 1 B-R; ESC 2023 Class I.
- **No routine multivessel PCI** in shock: ACC/AHA 2025 3: Harm B-R.
- **Microaxial flow pump** in selected STEMI-CS: ACC/AHA 2025 2a B-R.
- **Routine IABP or VA-ECMO**: ACC/AHA 2025 3: No Benefit B-R; ESC 2023 routine IABP III.
- **Norepinephrine** first vasopressor; inotrope for low output; avoid dopamine.
- Treat shock in a hub centre with a **shock team** (interventional, HF, critical care, cardiac surgery).

### Mechanical complications of MI
| Complication | Clue | Echo | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ventricular septal rupture | New harsh holosystolic murmur, thrill, biventricular failure | Shunt across the septum; O2 step-up RA -> RV | Surgery (or selected transcatheter closure); MCS/IABP bridge |
| Papillary muscle rupture | Sudden pulmonary oedema; murmur soft or absent | Flail leaflet, severe MR, hyperdynamic LV | Emergency mitral surgery; afterload reduction, MCS bridge |
| Free-wall rupture | Sudden PEA/tamponade | Effusion with tamponade, pseudoaneurysm | Emergency surgery |
| RV infarction | Inferior STEMI, V4R ST elevation, raised JVP, clear lungs | Dilated hypokinetic RV | Preload, avoid nitrates, pacing, reperfusion |
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Cardiogenic shock still kills about 40-50% of patients with MI-related shock. The exam rewards a structured approach: stage it, find a fixable cause, open the culprit artery, and know which trials killed routine IABP, routine ECMO and multivessel PCI.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Waiting for hypotension: **normotensive shock** with rising lactate is already stage C.
- Multivessel PCI at the index procedure in shock (CULPRIT-SHOCK: more death or renal replacement therapy).
- Routine IABP (IABP-SHOCK II) or routine ECMO (ECLS-SHOCK): no survival benefit.
- Dopamine as the first vasopressor.
- Nitrates or diuretics in RV infarction.
- Missing a **soft** murmur in papillary muscle rupture (the louder murmur is VSR).
- Needle drainage of haemopericardium from aortic dissection or free-wall rupture instead of surgery.
- Adding drug after drug in stage D instead of rethinking the cause and calling the shock team.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Day 3 after inferior MI, sudden pulmonary oedema, hyperdynamic LV, soft murmur -> **posteromedial papillary muscle rupture**.
- Day 4 after anterior MI, new loud holosystolic murmur with thrill, O2 step-up -> **VSR**.
- Inferior STEMI, hypotension after GTN, clear lungs, raised JVP -> **RV infarct**: fluids, not nitrates.
- STEMI with shock 20 hours after onset -> still **emergency PCI** (time limit does not apply in shock).
- 'Vasopressor of choice in cardiogenic shock?' -> **norepinephrine**.
- SCAI stage with lactate 9 and ongoing CPR -> **E**.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- SCAI A-E; B = instability without hypoperfusion; C = hypoperfusion + 1 intervention.
- Lactate ≥2 = hypoperfusion; ≥8 = extremis.
- Culprit-only PCI, any time from onset.
- DanGer-Shock: microaxial pump reduced death in selected STEMI-CS (cost: bleeding, limb ischaemia).
- Norepinephrine first; dobutamine/milrinone for low output.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
This guide walks one decision: a patient with possible ACS arrives - **which pathway, and how fast?** The first ECG (within 10 minutes of first medical contact) splits patients into STEMI (or a STEMI equivalent) and NSTE-ACS; troponin and risk then set the timing of angiography. Shock overrides everything.

*Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.*
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
Use the tree in order: **instability first, ECG second, time third, troponin and risk last.** Reperfusion in STEMI is never delayed for a troponin result.

[[figure:chest-pain-acs-algorithm]]

ESC 2023 and ACC/AHA 2025 agree on the architecture. The main difference is the clock: ACC/AHA counts from **first medical contact** (device <=90 min, <=120 min with transfer); ESC counts **120 min from STEMI diagnosis** when choosing PPCI over fibrinolysis, and ESC 2023 considers routine primary PCI up to 48 h after onset (IIa, B).
sections.title: Diagnostic reasoning

sections.body:
**Numbers and classes to know**

| Decision | ACC/AHA 2025 | ESC 2023 |
|---|---|---|
| ECG after first contact | Within 10 min (COR 1, B-NR) | Within 10 min |
| PPCI, STEMI <12 h | FMC-to-device <=90 min, <=120 min if transferred (COR 1, A) | PPCI if <120 min from diagnosis |
| Fibrinolysis | <12 h and expected PPCI delay >120 min, no contraindication (COR 1, A) | When PPCI not possible within 120 min of diagnosis |
| After fibrinolysis | Immediate transfer (1, A); angiography 2-24 h (1, B-R); rescue PCI if failed (1, B-R) | Angiography 2-24 h (I, A); rescue PCI if failed (I, A) |
| STEMI 12-24 h | PPCI reasonable (2a, B-NR) | Routine PPCI 12-48 h should be considered (IIa, B) |
| Stable, occluded artery >24 h | No PPCI (3: No benefit, B-R) | No routine PCI of an occluded IRA >48 h if asymptomatic (III, A) |
| ST depression only | No fibrinolysis (3: Harm, B-R) unless posterior STEMI | Same principle |
| NSTE-ACS, refractory angina or instability | Immediate invasive <2 h (1, C-LD) | Immediate <2 h (very high risk; I, C) |
| NSTE-ACS, high risk | Early invasive <24 h (2a, B-R) | Early <24 h should be considered (IIa, A) |
| hs-cTn repeat sample | 1-2 h (conventional cTn 3-6 h) (1, B-NR) | 0h/1h best, 0h/2h second best |
| ACS with shock | Culprit-vessel revascularization regardless of time (1, B-R); no routine non-culprit PCI (3: Harm, B-R) | Immediate invasive |
| Resuscitated arrest, comatose, stable, no STEMI | Immediate angiography not recommended (3: No benefit, A) | No routine immediate angiography (III, A) |
| MCS in STEMI shock | Microaxial pump in selected (2a, B-R); routine IABP/VA-ECMO no (3: No benefit, B-R) | - |

**STEMI ECG criteria** (ACC/AHA 2025 Table 3, from the 4th UDMI)

| Leads | ST elevation at J point, 2 contiguous leads |
|---|---|
| All leads except V2-V3 | >=1 mm |
| V2-V3, men >=40 y | >=2 mm |
| V2-V3, men <40 y | >=2.5 mm |
| V2-V3, women | >=1.5 mm |
| V7-V9 (posterior) | >=0.5 mm (>=1 mm in men <40 y) |

**Failed fibrinolysis** = <50% ST resolution in anterior leads or <70% in inferior leads, ongoing pain, or instability (ACC/AHA 2025 Sec 5.3.2).
sections.title: Severity classification

sections.body:
**ESC 2023 NSTE-ACS risk groups**

| Group | Criteria (any one) | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Very high risk | Haemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock; recurrent/refractory pain despite treatment; life-threatening arrhythmia; mechanical complication; ACS-related acute HF; recurrent dynamic ST/T changes | Immediate (<2 h) |
| High risk | NSTEMI confirmed by hs-cTn algorithm; dynamic ST/T changes; transient ST elevation; GRACE >140 | Early (<24 h) |
| Not high risk | None of the above | Selective invasive after non-invasive testing (ESC); invasive before discharge reasonable for intermediate risk (ACC/AHA) |
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Most ACS exam questions are really timing questions. If you can say, for any vignette, which pathway the patient is on and which clock is running, the drug and device details fall into place.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Waiting for troponin in STEMI.** Reperfusion is decided on the ECG; troponin never delays it.
- **Fibrinolysis for ST depression.** It is harmful (COR 3: Harm) unless true posterior STEMI is suspected - record V7-V9 first.
- **New LBBB = STEMI.** Not on its own: ACC/AHA 2025 says new LBBB is not diagnostic in isolation and is not a STEMI equivalent when asymptomatic; it matters with ongoing ischaemic symptoms or instability.
- **Multivessel PCI in shock.** Culprit-only at the index procedure (CULPRIT-SHOCK); non-culprit PCI in shock is harmful.
- **Routine IABP in shock.** No survival benefit (IABP-SHOCK II); the microaxial pump is 2a only in *selected* STEMI shock and has more bleeding and limb ischaemia.
- **Mixing the clocks.** ACC/AHA's 90/120 min are from first medical contact; ESC's 120 min decision is from diagnosis.
- **Opening a stable occluded artery after 24-48 h** - no benefit (OAT).
- **Immediate angiography for every resuscitated arrest.** Comatose, electrically and haemodynamically stable, no STEMI: not recommended (ACC/AHA 2025 3: No benefit, A; ESC 2023 III A). With STEMI on the ECG: PPCI.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- Rural hospital without a cath lab, transfer >2 h, symptoms 3 h, no contraindication -> **fibrinolysis then transfer, angiography 2-24 h** (pharmaco-invasive). Very relevant to Indonesian regional hospitals.
- Inferior STEMI + hypotension + clear lungs -> right-sided leads (V4R), think RV infarction: fluids, avoid nitrates.
- ST depression V1-V3 with tall R in V1-V2 -> posterior MI -> V7-V9.
- 60 min after lysis, pain persists and ST resolution 30% -> **rescue PCI**.
- NSTEMI with recurrent pain and VT on medical therapy -> immediate (<2 h) angiography.
- NSTEMI, pain-free, GRACE 150 -> angiography within 24 h.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Three clocks:** ECG <=10 min; FMC-to-device <=90 min (<=120 min with transfer); angiography 2-24 h after lysis.
- **PPCI beats lysis when timely**; each 30-min PPCI delay raises 1-year mortality ~7.5% (relative).
- **NSTE-ACS timing ladder:** immediate <2 h (very high risk) -> early <24 h (high risk) -> before discharge / selective (others).
- **hs-cTn:** rise and/or fall with >=1 value >99th percentile URL; repeat at 1-2 h; assay-specific thresholds; single-sample rule-out only >=3 h after onset.
- **Fifth Universal Definition of MI (ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF 2026)** replaces numbered types with clinical categories: primary (formerly type 1), secondary (formerly type 2) and procedure-related MI (formerly types 4 and 5; type 3 is no longer a separate category), with sex-specific 99th-percentile troponin limits; MINOCA's 'I' now means 'injury' as a working diagnosis.
- PERKI's ACS guidance generally follows ESC; check the current PERKI edition for local adaptations (not verified here).
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Decision guide: chest pain and suspected ACS (STEMI vs NSTE-ACS)

sections.body:
The surface ECG records the **summed electrical activity of millions of myocytes** as voltage differences between electrodes on the skin. Each **lead** is a pair of electrode positions (or one electrode against a reference) that defines an **axis** with a positive and a negative end. A lead records:
- an **upright** deflection when the net depolarisation vector points **toward** its positive end,
- a **negative** deflection when the vector points **away**,
- a **biphasic / equiphasic** deflection when the vector is **perpendicular** to it.

Size depends on the **amount of muscle** depolarising, the **direction** (the projection is proportional to the cosine of the angle between the vector and the lead) and what lies between heart and skin (fluid, air and fat reduce it).
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
### The dipole
At rest the outside of every myocyte is **positive**. When a cell depolarises its outside becomes **negative**. A spreading **wavefront** therefore has negative charge behind it and positive charge ahead: a **dipole** whose positive head points in the direction of spread.

[[figure:ecg-dipole-lead]]

**Repolarisation** is the reverse dipole (positive behind, negative ahead), so a repolarisation wave moving toward an electrode would write a **negative** wave. In the ventricles, however, repolarisation runs the **opposite way to depolarisation**: **epicardium to endocardium**, because epicardial action potentials are shorter. Two reversals cancel, so the normal **T wave has the same direction as the QRS** in most leads.

### The sequence of vectors
1. **Atria** - the SA node fires at the high RA; the wave spreads down and to the left (P axis about +60 degrees): **P upright in II, inverted in aVR**. In V1 the P is often biphasic (RA first, then LA).
2. **AV node and His-Purkinje** - too little tissue to register: the flat **PR segment**.
3. **Septum** - activated first, from the **left** bundle, so the vector points **left to right**: a small **r in V1** and a small **"septal" q in I, aVL, V5-V6**.
4. **Free walls** - the thicker LV dominates; the main vector points **left, inferior and posterior**: tall **R in V5-V6**, deep **S in V1-V2**.
5. **Basal parts** last: a small terminal s in the lateral leads.
6. **Plateau** - every ventricular cell is depolarised at the same level, so no current flows: the isoelectric **ST segment**.
7. **Repolarisation** - the **T wave**; the **U wave** follows (mechanism debated; prominent in hypokalaemia).
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
### Leads
- **Limb (frontal plane):** bipolar I (LA+ vs RA-), II (LL+ vs RA-), III (LL+ vs LA-); augmented unipolar aVR, aVL, aVF. **Einthoven's law: II = I + III.** Also aVR + aVL + aVF = 0.
- **Precordial (horizontal plane):** V1-V6, each recorded against Wilson's central terminal (the average of the three limb electrodes).

| Lead | Positive pole (degrees) | Looks at |
|---|---|---|
| I | 0 | High lateral |
| aVL | -30 | High lateral |
| II | +60 | Inferior |
| aVF | +90 | Inferior |
| III | +120 | Inferior |
| aVR | -150 (+210) | Cavity / right upper |
| V1-V2 | Horizontal plane | Septum, RV |
| V3-V4 | Horizontal plane | Anterior |
| V5-V6 | Horizontal plane | Lateral |

### Waves and intervals

[[figure:ecg-intervals]]

| Component | What it represents | Normal adult value |
|---|---|---|
| P wave | Atrial depolarisation | < 120 ms; < 2.5 mm tall in II |
| PR interval | Start of atrial depolarisation to start of ventricular depolarisation (atria + **AV node delay** + His-Purkinje) | 120-200 ms |
| PR segment | AV nodal and His conduction (atrial repolarisation hidden here) | Isoelectric |
| QRS | Ventricular depolarisation | < 120 ms |
| J point | End of QRS, start of ST | On the baseline |
| ST segment | Plateau (phase 2): all ventricular cells depolarised | Isoelectric |
| T wave | Ventricular repolarisation (phase 3) | Same direction as the QRS in most leads |
| QT interval | Whole ventricular depolarisation + repolarisation | QTc prolonged if > 450 ms (men), > 460 ms (women); > 500 ms = high torsades risk |

Paper: **25 mm/s and 10 mm/mV**. One small box = **40 ms**, one large box = **200 ms**. Heart rate ~ **300 / number of large boxes** (or 1500 / small boxes) between R waves. **QTc (Bazett) = QT / square root of RR (in seconds)**; Bazett over-corrects at fast rates.

### QRS axis

[[figure:ecg-hexaxial-axis]]

- **Normal: -30 to +90 degrees.** Left axis deviation: beyond -30. Right axis deviation: beyond +90. Extreme axis: -90 to 180.
- **Quick method:** leads I and aVF both positive = normal. I positive, aVF negative: look at II (positive = still normal, 0 to -30; negative = LAD). I negative, aVF positive = RAD. Both negative = extreme.
- **Refine:** find the most equiphasic limb lead; the axis is perpendicular to it, pointing toward the lead where the QRS is upright.
- **LAD causes:** left anterior fascicular block (axis -45 or beyond, qR in aVL, rS in II/III/aVF), inferior MI, LVH, primum ASD, some pre-excitation.
- **RAD causes:** RVH, acute RV strain (PE), left posterior fascicular block (a diagnosis of exclusion), lateral MI, dextrocardia or arm-lead reversal, secundum ASD; can be normal in children and tall thin adults.

### R-wave progression
Across V1 to V6 the R wave grows and the S wave shrinks because the electrodes move from facing the RV (vector moving away) to facing the LV (vector approaching). The **transition (R = S) is normally at V3-V4**.
- **Poor R-wave progression** (small R in V1-V3): anterior MI, LVH, LBBB, COPD, high lead placement.
- **Tall R in V1 (early transition):** RBBB, RVH, posterior MI, pre-excitation with a left-sided pathway, HCM, dextroposition.
sections.title: ECG

sections.body: Every ECG pattern you will be asked about, from bundle branch block to infarct localisation, hypertrophy and axis deviation, is the vector rules applied to a changed sequence of activation. If you can predict the normal ECG from the dipole, the lead axes and the order of activation, abnormal tracings become reasoning rather than pattern memory.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- The **PR interval** includes atrial depolarisation; the **PR segment** does not. PR depression in pericarditis is a PR **segment** change.
- The **ST segment is isoelectric because no current flows**, not because nothing is happening: cells are in their plateau.
- An inverted T wave in **aVR** is normal (everything points away from the right shoulder), and T inversion in **III** or **V1** alone can be normal.
- **Left axis deviation is beyond -30**, not "anything negative": an axis of -10 is normal.
- Lead **II negative with I positive** separates true LAD from a normal leftward axis between 0 and -30.
- **Arm-lead reversal** mimics RAD with an inverted P and QRS in I; check that P is upright in II and inverted in aVR.
- **Bazett** inflates QTc at high heart rates: re-measure when the rate is slower or use another formula.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Leads I positive, aVF negative, II negative" -> **left axis deviation** (e.g. left anterior fascicular block).
- "Lead I negative, aVF positive in a young patient with a loud P2" -> **RAD from RV pressure overload**.
- "Equiphasic QRS in aVL" -> axis about **+60** (perpendicular to -30; II upright).
- "Small q waves in V5-V6 in a healthy person" -> **normal septal depolarisation**.
- "Tall R in V1 with ST depression V1-V3" -> think **posterior MI** (mirror image), not only RVH or RBBB.
- "Which interval is mainly the AV node?" -> **PR interval / PR segment**.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Toward the positive pole = upright; away = negative; perpendicular = equiphasic.**
- Ventricular repolarisation runs **epicardium to endocardium**, so the normal T wave is **concordant** with the QRS.
- Septal depolarisation is **left to right**: septal q in I, aVL, V5-V6 and the r in V1.
- **Hexaxial:** I 0, aVL -30, II +60, aVF +90, III +120, aVR -150. **II = I + III.**
- **Normal axis -30 to +90**; I and aVF method; equiphasic lead is perpendicular.
- **PR 120-200 ms (mostly AV node delay); QRS < 120 ms; QTc long > 450 (men) / > 460 (women) ms.**
- 1 small box = 40 ms; 1 large box = 200 ms; HR ~ 300 / large boxes.
- R-wave transition normally **V3-V4**.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: ECG genesis: vectors, intervals and axis

sections.body:
**Excitation-contraction (E-C) coupling** is the chain of events that turns the action potential into a contraction, with **calcium** as the messenger. **Relaxation is the reverse: removing calcium**, and it is just as active and energy-dependent.

- **Inotropy** = the force and speed of contraction at a given load (contractility).
- **Lusitropy** = the speed and completeness of **myocardial relaxation**.
- **Chronotropy** = heart rate; **dromotropy** = conduction velocity (mainly the AV node).
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
[[figure:ec-coupling]]

### Contraction: calcium-induced calcium release
1. The action potential travels along the sarcolemma and down the **T-tubules** (dense in ventricular myocytes).
