2. During the **plateau (phase 2)**, **L-type Ca2+ channels** (dihydropyridine receptors) open and a **small trigger** of Ca2+ enters the narrow cleft between the T-tubule and the junctional SR.
3. That Ca2+ opens the **ryanodine receptors (RyR2)** on the SR: **calcium-induced calcium release (CICR)**. Most of the systolic Ca2+ comes from the SR, not from outside.
4. Free cytosolic Ca2+ rises roughly tenfold (from about 0.1 to about 1 micromolar) and binds **troponin C**; troponin I releases actin, **tropomyosin** moves and **myosin** heads form cross-bridges; ATP hydrolysis drives the power stroke.

**Cardiac vs skeletal muscle:** in skeletal muscle the DHPR is mechanically linked to RyR1 and contraction does not need Ca2+ entry. Cardiac muscle **needs extracellular Ca2+** to trigger release, so **calcium channel blockers are negatively inotropic** and contraction is **graded** by how much Ca2+ is released and how sensitive the myofilaments are (including length-dependent activation: the cellular basis of Frank-Starling).

### Relaxation: getting calcium out of the cytosol
- **SERCA2a** pumps Ca2+ back into the SR (the larger share; about 70% in human ventricle). It uses **ATP**.
- **Phospholamban (PLB)** is SERCA's brake. When PLB is phosphorylated (by **PKA** or CaMKII) the brake comes off: faster Ca2+ reuptake (**lusitropy**) and a fuller SR for the next beat (**inotropy**).
- The **Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX)** extrudes most of the rest (about 28%): 3 Na+ in for 1 Ca2+ out, driven by the Na+ gradient that the **Na+/K+-ATPase** maintains. At steady state the Ca2+ that entered via L-type channels leaves via NCX each beat.
- Minor routes: sarcolemmal Ca2+-ATPase and mitochondria.
- Myosin needs **ATP to detach from actin**, so ATP depletion stiffens the muscle (rigor). This is why **relaxation fails early in ischaemia**: diastolic dysfunction comes before systolic dysfunction, ECG change and angina in the ischaemic cascade.

### Beta-adrenergic stimulation
Beta-1 receptor -> Gs -> adenylyl cyclase -> **cAMP -> PKA**, which phosphorylates:

| PKA target | Effect | Result |
|---|---|---|
| L-type Ca2+ channel | More Ca2+ entry per beat | Bigger trigger and Ca2+ transient: inotropy |
| Phospholamban | Releases the SERCA brake | Faster Ca2+ reuptake (lusitropy) and more SR Ca2+ (inotropy) |
| Troponin I | Lowers myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity | Ca2+ leaves troponin C sooner: faster relaxation |
| RyR2 | Changes release channel gating | Contributes to larger release (and to leak in disease) |
| Myosin-binding protein C | Faster cross-bridge cycling | Faster force development and relaxation |
| Nodal L-type Ca2+ channels (plus cAMP binding directly to HCN/If channels, not via PKA) | Steeper phase 4, faster AV nodal conduction | Chronotropy and dromotropy |

So a catecholamine makes the heart contract **harder and faster and relax faster**, which preserves diastolic filling time at high heart rates.

**Force-frequency relation (Bowditch staircase):** in a normal heart a faster rate increases force (more Ca2+ entry per minute loads the SR) and accelerates relaxation. In heart failure it is flat or negative.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
### Measuring inotropy and lusitropy
- **Inotropy:** slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relation (**Ees**, load-independent), peak **+dP/dt**; ejection fraction is load-dependent.
- **Lusitropy (active relaxation):** **tau**, the time constant of isovolumic LV pressure fall (prolonged in HFpEF; a value above 48 ms was used as abnormal in the 2007 ESC consensus), peak **-dP/dt**, isovolumic relaxation time, and on echo the mitral annular **e' velocity**.
- **Passive stiffness (compliance)** is a different property: the slope of the **end-diastolic pressure-volume relation (EDPVR)**, set by wall thickness, fibrosis and **titin**.

### From cell to diastolic dysfunction
Diastolic dysfunction = **slow or incomplete active relaxation** plus **increased passive stiffness**, so the ventricle needs a higher filling pressure to reach a normal volume.
- **Slow relaxation:** less SERCA2a, relatively more PLB, less PLB phosphorylation, ischaemia (no ATP), hypertrophy, ageing, hypothyroidism.
- **More stiffness:** LVH, interstitial fibrosis, a shift to stiffer titin isoforms and reduced titin phosphorylation.
- **Tachycardia** shortens diastole; a slowly relaxing ventricle may not finish relaxing before the next beat, and **loss of the atrial kick (AF)** removes a large part of filling. This is why patients with HFpEF, LVH or HCM decompensate with fast AF.

Echo pattern (ASE/EACVI 2016): impaired relaxation (E/A low, long deceleration time, reduced e') -> pseudonormal -> restrictive (E/A >= 2, short deceleration time). Markers of raised filling pressure: **average E/e' > 14**, **septal e' < 7 cm/s or lateral e' < 10 cm/s**, **TR velocity > 2.8 m/s**, **LA volume index > 34 mL/m2**.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body:
**Drugs that act on E-C coupling:**
- **Beta-agonists (dobutamine)** and **PDE3 inhibitors (milrinone)** raise cAMP: positive inotropy and lusitropy; milrinone also vasodilates (an "inodilator"). Both raise myocardial O2 demand and arrhythmia risk.
- **Digoxin** blocks the Na+/K+-ATPase -> more intracellular Na+ -> less Ca2+ out via NCX -> more SR Ca2+: modest inotropy, plus vagal slowing of the AV node; Ca2+ overload causes DAD arrhythmias in toxicity.
- **Levosimendan** sensitises troponin C to Ca2+ (inotropy without raising Ca2+) and opens K-ATP channels (vasodilation).
- **Omecamtiv mecarbil** (cardiac myosin activator) lengthens systolic ejection without raising Ca2+; **mavacamten** (cardiac myosin inhibitor) reduces hypercontractility in obstructive HCM.
- **Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers** and **beta-blockers** are negatively inotropic; beta-blockers help diastolic filling mainly by **slowing the heart** (longer diastole), not by speeding relaxation.
sections.title: Management principles

sections.body: Every inotrope, every negative inotrope and most of the physiology of HFpEF sit on this one calcium cycle. Knowing where Ca2+ enters, where it is stored, what releases and removes it and how PKA tunes each step explains digoxin toxicity, why ischaemia stiffens the ventricle first, why tachycardia hurts the stiff heart and how the newer myosin drugs differ from catecholamines.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- **Relaxation is not passive**: it costs ATP, so ischaemia impairs relaxation before contraction.
- **Lusitropy (active relaxation) is not compliance (passive stiffness)**: tau and e' vs the EDPVR slope.
- **Troponin I phosphorylation lowers Ca2+ sensitivity** - it speeds relaxation; it does not increase force.
- **Phosphorylated phospholamban stops inhibiting SERCA**; dephosphorylated PLB is the brake.
- Most systolic Ca2+ comes from the **SR**, not from the extracellular fluid, although the extracellular trigger is essential.
- **NCX moves 3 Na+ for 1 Ca2+**: it is electrogenic, which is why it can depolarise the cell (DADs).
- Levosimendan and omecamtiv work **without raising intracellular Ca2+**; dobutamine, milrinone and digoxin raise it.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Mechanism of the positive inotropic effect of digoxin" -> **Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition -> reduced Ca2+ extrusion by NCX -> more SR Ca2+**.
- "Which protein's phosphorylation by PKA speeds relaxation?" -> **phospholamban** (and troponin I).
- "Earliest abnormality in the ischaemic cascade" -> **diastolic dysfunction (impaired relaxation)**.
- "Why does fast AF decompensate a patient with LVH?" -> **shortened diastole + loss of atrial kick in a stiff, slowly relaxing ventricle**.
- "Calcium sensitiser used in acute HF" -> **levosimendan**.
- "Why are verapamil and diltiazem negatively inotropic?" -> **less trigger Ca2+ through L-type channels -> less CICR**.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **CICR:** L-type Ca2+ trigger (phase 2) -> RyR2 release from the SR -> Ca2+ binds **troponin C**.
- Cardiac contraction **needs extracellular Ca2+** (unlike skeletal muscle) and is **graded**.
- **Relaxation is active:** SERCA2a (~70%), NCX (~28%); ATP is needed for SERCA and for cross-bridge detachment.
- **Phospholamban brakes SERCA; PKA phosphorylation releases it** -> lusitropy + inotropy.
- **Beta-stimulation targets:** L-type channel, PLB, troponin I, RyR2, MyBP-C.
- **Digoxin:** Na+/K+-ATPase block -> NCX extrudes less Ca2+ -> more SR Ca2+.
- **Diastolic dysfunction appears first in the ischaemic cascade.** Tau, -dP/dt and e' measure relaxation; EDPVR measures stiffness.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
Exercise is the largest physiological stress the cardiovascular system meets. Its job is to deliver oxygen to working muscle, captured by the **Fick principle**:

`VO2 = CO x (CaO2 - CvO2) = HR x SV x (a-vO2 difference)`

- **VO2max** is the highest oxygen uptake a person can reach: VO2 plateaus despite a rising workload. When no plateau is reached the highest value is called **peak VO2**.
- **1 MET** = resting oxygen uptake, about **3.5 mL O2/kg/min**.
- Typical VO2max: roughly **35-45 mL/kg/min** in healthy young untrained men (lower in women and with age); elite endurance athletes reach about **70-85 mL/kg/min**.
- In a healthy person, VO2max is limited mainly by **maximal cardiac output** (central delivery), not by the lungs.

**Dynamic (isotonic) exercise** (running, cycling, swimming) moves large muscle groups rhythmically and is a **volume load**. **Static (isometric) exercise** (lifting, handgrip) is sustained contraction without movement and is a **pressure load**.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
### How the responses are driven
- **Central command**: the motor cortex drives cardiovascular centres in parallel with the muscles, so HR rises at the very start of exercise.
- **Exercise pressor reflex**: muscle mechanoreceptors and metaboreceptors (group III/IV afferents) increase sympathetic outflow.
- **Baroreflex resetting** to a higher operating pressure, so BP can rise without a reflex slowing of the heart.
- **Local metabolic vasodilatation** in working muscle (K+, adenosine, H+, CO2, NO, low PO2) overrides sympathetic vasoconstriction there (**functional sympatholysis**), while non-working beds (gut, kidney, inactive muscle) constrict.

HR rises first by **vagal withdrawal** (roughly up to about 100 bpm), then by **sympathetic** stimulation.

### Dynamic vs static exercise
| Variable | Dynamic (running, cycling) | Static (lifting, handgrip) |
|---|---|---|
| Heart rate | ↑↑ (linear with workload) | ↑ (modest) |
| Stroke volume | ↑ then plateaus | Little change |
| Cardiac output | ↑↑↑ (about 4-fold or more) | ↑ (modest) |
| Systolic BP | ↑↑ | ↑↑ |
| Diastolic BP | Unchanged or slightly ↓ | ↑↑ |
| Mean arterial pressure | Modest ↑ | Marked ↑ |
| SVR | ↓↓ (muscle vasodilatation) | Unchanged or ↑ (contracting muscle compresses its vessels) |
| Load on the LV | Volume load | Pressure load |
| Classic training pattern | Eccentric remodelling, larger cavity | Mild concentric wall thickening |

### Training adaptations (endurance)
- **VO2max rises** mainly through a higher **maximal stroke volume** (plasma volume expansion, larger and more compliant LV) and a wider **a-vO2 difference** (more capillaries and mitochondria in muscle).
- **Maximal HR does not rise** with training; it falls with age (about **220 - age**, or 208 - 0.7 x age by Tanaka).
- **Resting and submaximal HR fall** (higher vagal tone, larger SV): the trained heart does the same work at a lower rate.

### Deconditioning
Bed rest and inactivity reverse these changes: plasma volume and stroke volume fall, VO2max drops, the resting and submaximal HR rise, and **orthostatic intolerance** appears. In heart failure, much of the exercise limitation is **peripheral** (skeletal-muscle deconditioning, endothelial dysfunction), which is why **exercise training (cardiac rehabilitation)** improves peak VO2 even when EF does not change.
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
### The responses to rising dynamic workload
[[figure:exercise-responses]]

- **Heart rate** rises almost **linearly** with workload and VO2 up to the maximum.
- **Stroke volume** rises (more venous return -> Frank-Starling, plus more inotropy -> smaller end-systolic volume) and in untrained people **plateaus at about 40-60% of VO2max**, as the shorter diastole limits filling. Further output then comes from HR.
- **Cardiac output** rises from about 5 L/min to about **20-25 L/min** in a fit young adult (**up to 35-40 L/min** in elite endurance athletes).
- **Venous return** keeps pace through the **skeletal-muscle pump**, the **respiratory pump** and sympathetic **venoconstriction** (raises mean systemic filling pressure).
- **a-vO2 difference** widens from about **5 mL O2/dL** at rest to about **15 mL O2/dL or more** at peak: more capillaries open, the oxyhaemoglobin curve shifts right (heat, CO2, H+, 2,3-BPG), and muscle extracts more.
- **Systolic BP** rises progressively; **diastolic BP** stays about the same or falls slightly; **SVR falls** steeply.
- **Blood-flow redistribution**: working muscle receives most of the output at peak exercise; coronary flow rises in proportion to myocardial O2 demand; skin flow rises for heat loss; renal and splanchnic flow fall; cerebral flow stays roughly constant.

[[figure:fick-vo2]]

### Exercise testing hooks
- **Chronotropic incompetence**: failure to reach **85% of age-predicted maximal HR**, or a **chronotropic index < 0.80** (fraction of HR reserve used; **< 0.62** on β-blockers). Causes: sinus node disease, β-blockers, heart failure, diabetic autonomic neuropathy. It independently predicts mortality.
- **Heart-rate recovery (HRR)**: the fall in HR in the first minute after stopping. Abnormal = **≤ 12 bpm** with an upright cool-down (≤ 18 bpm if the patient lies down at once). Reflects slow **vagal reactivation**; predicts mortality.
- **Exercise-induced hypotension** (SBP falls as the workload rises) is a high-risk finding: think severe multivessel or left main CAD, severe LV dysfunction or severe outflow obstruction. Stop the test.
- **CPET in heart failure**: a **respiratory exchange ratio (RER) > 1.05** shows adequate effort; **peak VO2 ≤ 14 mL/kg/min** (≤ 12 on β-blockers) supports referral for transplant listing (ISHLT).
- **HFpEF**: a normal resting PCWP can rise to **≥ 25 mmHg** during exercise; that is the invasive diagnostic criterion for exercise-induced elevated filling pressure.

### Athlete's heart vs hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
| Feature | Favours athlete's heart | Favours HCM |
|---|---|---|
| Maximal LV wall thickness | Usually ≤ 12 mm (13-15 mm is the grey zone; > 11 mm is unusual in women) | ≥ 15 mm (≥ 13 mm in a relative of a patient with HCM) |
| Pattern of hypertrophy | Symmetric, homogeneous | Asymmetric (often septal), apical or patchy |
| LV cavity | Enlarged (LVEDD often > 55 mm) | Small or normal (often < 45 mm) |
| Diastolic function | Normal (normal e′) | Impaired (low e′, high E/e′) |
| Outflow obstruction, SAM | Absent | May be present |
| ECG | Isolated QRS voltage criteria, sinus bradycardia, early repolarisation | Pathological Q waves, deep lateral or inferolateral T-wave inversion, ST depression, LBBB |
| CMR | No late gadolinium enhancement | Patchy mid-wall LGE (often at RV insertion points) |
| Peak VO2 | High (> 50 mL/kg/min or > 20% above predicted) | Normal or reduced |
| Detraining (about 3 months) | Wall thickness regresses | No regression |
| Family history and genetics | Negative | HCM or sudden death in relatives; sarcomere gene variant |
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Exercise is the stress test the circulation was designed for, and it reveals problems that are hidden at rest: ischaemia, chronotropic failure, HFpEF, valve disease and the limits of a failing ventricle. The Fick equation tells you which link (HR, SV or extraction) is failing, and the athlete-vs-HCM distinction is a classic exam and pre-participation screening question with life-or-death consequences.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- Diastolic BP does **not** rise much with dynamic exercise; a large DBP rise suggests a static (isometric) component.
- **SVR falls** during dynamic exercise even though MAP rises: the rise in CO outweighs the fall in resistance.
- Training does **not** increase maximal HR; it increases maximal SV and lowers the HR at any given submaximal workload.
- Peak VO2 is meaningless if the effort was submaximal: check that **RER > 1.05** before using it to grade heart failure.
- A thick wall with a **large** cavity and **normal** diastolic function is athletic until proven otherwise; a thick wall with a **small** cavity and **impaired** relaxation is HCM until proven otherwise.
- A fall in systolic BP during exercise is not "fatigue": it is a high-risk ischaemic marker.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Main determinant of VO2max in a healthy adult?" -> **maximal cardiac output** (specifically maximal stroke volume).
- "Haemodynamic change with isometric handgrip?" -> **↑ SBP, ↑ DBP, ↑ afterload** (also increases most left-sided regurgitant murmurs).
- "Septum 14 mm, LVEDD 58 mm, normal e′, no LGE, regresses after detraining" -> **athlete's heart**.
- "HR rises only to 60% of predicted on treadmill, no β-blocker" -> **chronotropic incompetence** (often sinus node disease).
- "HR falls by 8 bpm one minute after exercise" -> **abnormal heart-rate recovery**, adverse prognosis.
- "HFrEF patient on β-blocker, RER 1.12, peak VO2 11 mL/kg/min" -> meets the **transplant-listing** threshold.
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- **Fick**: `VO2 = HR x SV x (CaO2 - CvO2)`; 1 MET = 3.5 mL/kg/min.
- Dynamic exercise: **↑ HR, ↑ SV, ↑↑ CO, ↑ SBP, DBP ~ unchanged, ↓↓ SVR** (volume load). Static: **↑↑ SBP and DBP**, little SV change (pressure load).
- SV plateaus at about 40-60% of VO2max in untrained subjects; later increases in CO come from HR.
- a-vO2 difference roughly **triples** (about 5 -> 15 mL/dL) at peak.
- Training raises VO2max mainly via **↑ maximal SV**; **maximal HR is not trainable**.
- **Chronotropic incompetence**: < 85% age-predicted max HR or chronotropic index < 0.80.
- **Abnormal HRR**: ≤ 12 bpm in the first minute (upright).
- Peak VO2 **≤ 14 mL/kg/min (≤ 12 on β-blockers)** with RER > 1.05 -> transplant evaluation.
- Athlete vs HCM: **cavity size, diastolic function, LGE, detraining** are the discriminators in the 13-15 mm grey zone.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

sections.body:
In the fetus the **placenta**, not the lung, is the organ of gas exchange. The fetal circulation is built to send the best-oxygenated blood to the **heart and brain** and to bypass the fluid-filled lungs and, partly, the liver. It works as **two ventricles in parallel** (not in series as after birth), linked by three shunts:
- **Ductus venosus** - umbilical vein -> IVC (bypasses the liver).
- **Foramen ovale** - right atrium -> left atrium (bypasses the right ventricle and lungs).
- **Ductus arteriosus** - pulmonary trunk -> descending aorta (bypasses the lungs).

At birth the lungs take over, the placenta is removed and within minutes to days the circulation converts to the adult series pattern.
sections.title: Definition

sections.body:
### The path of the blood
1. **Umbilical vein** (one vein) carries the most oxygenated blood from the placenta (saturation about **80-85%**, PO2 only about 30-35 mmHg).
2. Part of it passes through the **liver**; part bypasses it through the **ductus venosus** into the IVC.
3. In the right atrium this well-oxygenated stream is directed by the **Eustachian valve** and the edge of the atrial septum (crista dividens) **across the foramen ovale** into the left atrium.
4. **LA -> LV -> ascending aorta** (saturation about **65%**) -> **coronary arteries and brain** (the arch vessels) get the best blood.
5. Desaturated **SVC** blood (about 40%) streams instead through the tricuspid valve into the **RV -> pulmonary trunk**.
6. Because **pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is very high** (collapsed, fluid-filled lungs and hypoxic vasoconstriction), only a small fraction (roughly 10-20%) of RV output enters the lungs. The rest crosses the **ductus arteriosus** to the **descending aorta** (saturation about 55-60%).
7. Two **umbilical arteries** (from the internal iliac arteries) return blood to the low-resistance placenta.

[[figure:fetal-circulation]]

### Why the fetus copes with a low PO2
- **Fetal haemoglobin (HbF)** binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its oxygen-dissociation curve is **shifted left** (higher O2 affinity, lower P50) and it loads O2 at placental PO2.
- High haemoglobin concentration and high cardiac output per kilogram.
- The **RV ejects more than the LV** in the fetus (right-ventricular dominance); the placenta is the lowest-resistance bed in the body, so systemic resistance is low.

### The three shunts and their fate
| Shunt | Connects | Purpose in the fetus | Closure after birth | Adult remnant |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ductus venosus | Umbilical vein -> IVC | Bypasses the liver | Functional within days (loss of umbilical flow) | Ligamentum venosum |
| Foramen ovale | RA -> LA | Sends oxygenated IVC blood to the LV and brain | Functional within minutes to hours (LA pressure > RA); anatomical fusion over months | Fossa ovalis; patent (PFO) in about 25% of adults |
| Ductus arteriosus | Pulmonary trunk -> descending aorta | Bypasses the high-resistance lungs | Functional usually within 1-3 days in term infants; fibrosis over weeks | Ligamentum arteriosum |
| Umbilical vein / arteries | Placenta <-> fetus | Gas and nutrient exchange | Constrict when the cord is clamped | Ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) / medial umbilical ligaments |
sections.title: Pathophysiology

sections.body:
### What changes at birth, and why
1. **Clamping the cord** removes the low-resistance placenta -> **SVR rises**; umbilical venous return stops -> **RA pressure falls**.
2. **First breaths** expand the lungs; alveolar O2 rises; oxygen, nitric oxide and prostacyclin dilate the pulmonary arterioles -> **PVR falls dramatically** -> pulmonary blood flow rises many-fold.
3. More pulmonary venous return raises **LA pressure above RA pressure** -> the flap of septum primum is pushed against septum secundum -> **foramen ovale closes** functionally.
4. With PVR now below SVR, flow through the still-open **ductus arteriosus reverses** (becomes left-to-right). The duct then **constricts**, because of the **rise in PaO2** and the **fall in prostaglandin E2** (the placental source is gone and the lungs now metabolise PGE2).
5. The **ductus venosus** closes after umbilical flow stops.

[[figure:neonatal-transition]]

PVR keeps falling over the following weeks (smooth-muscle regression in the small pulmonary arteries), reaching near-adult levels at about 6-8 weeks. That is why a **large VSD or PDA** often becomes symptomatic (heart failure, increasing left-to-right shunt) at **4-8 weeks** rather than at birth.

### Drugs that act on the ductus
**Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil)** keeps the duct open in **duct-dependent lesions**. Side effects: **apnoea**, fever, flushing, hypotension.
- **Duct-dependent pulmonary flow**: pulmonary atresia, critical pulmonary stenosis, tricuspid atresia with restricted pulmonary flow.
- **Duct-dependent systemic flow**: hypoplastic left heart syndrome, critical coarctation, interrupted aortic arch, critical aortic stenosis.
- **Mixing**: transposition of the great arteries (often with balloon atrial septostomy).

**Closing the duct**
- **COX inhibitors (indomethacin, ibuprofen) and paracetamol** promote closure of a haemodynamically significant **PDA in preterm infants** (the preterm duct is less sensitive to oxygen and more sensitive to PGE2).
- Maternal **NSAIDs in late pregnancy** can constrict the duct in utero.

### Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)
PVR fails to fall, so pulmonary pressure stays at or above systemic pressure and blood shunts **right-to-left** across the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus -> severe hypoxaemia with a structurally normal heart.
- **Causes**: meconium aspiration, sepsis/pneumonia, perinatal asphyxia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, respiratory distress syndrome, idiopathic.
- **Clue**: **differential cyanosis** - pre-ductal SpO2 (right hand) higher than post-ductal SpO2 (foot) when the shunt is at ductal level.
- **Treatment**: oxygen, optimal ventilation and lung recruitment (surfactant when indicated), correct acidosis, hypothermia and hypoglycaemia, support systemic BP, **inhaled nitric oxide**, ECMO when refractory.
sections.title: Hemodynamics

sections.body: Almost every congenital heart lesion declares itself during the transition from fetal to neonatal circulation: duct-dependent lesions crash when the ductus closes, shunt lesions appear as PVR falls, and PPHN mimics cyanotic heart disease. Knowing the fetal pathways, the saturations in each chamber and the forces that close each shunt lets you predict the timing and the physiology of these presentations and the drugs that help.
sections.title: Why (the reasoning behind it)

sections.body:
- The **umbilical vein** carries oxygenated blood and the **umbilical arteries** carry deoxygenated blood (the reverse of the adult naming habit).
- Most RV output in the fetus goes through the **ductus**, not the lungs.
- Fetal flow across the ductus is **pulmonary -> aorta**; after birth it reverses to **aorta -> pulmonary** (the PDA murmur and left-to-right shunt).
- The foramen ovale closes because of the **pressure change** (LA > RA), not because of oxygen; the ductus closes mainly because of **oxygen and the fall in PGE2**.
- **Reverse differential cyanosis** (foot pinker than hand) points to **transposition of the great arteries** with pulmonary hypertension or arch obstruction, not to simple PPHN.
- Giving oxygen alone does not open a duct; in a duct-dependent lesion **PGE1** is the life-saving drug.
sections.title: Common traps

sections.body:
- "Vessel with the highest PO2 in the fetus?" -> **umbilical vein**.
- "Neonate with HLHS deteriorates on day 2" -> **ductal closure**; start **PGE1**.
- "Infant on PGE1 develops apnoea" -> known side effect; be ready to ventilate.
- "Preterm with bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, continuous murmur" -> **PDA**; COX inhibitor or paracetamol.
- "Term baby after meconium aspiration, right-hand SpO2 95%, foot 80%, normal heart on echo" -> **PPHN** with ductal right-to-left shunt.
- "Large VSD silent at birth, heart failure at 6 weeks" -> **falling PVR** increases the left-to-right shunt.
- "Remnant of the ductus arteriosus" -> **ligamentum arteriosum** (near the left recurrent laryngeal nerve).
sections.title: PPDS clues

sections.body:
- Highest O2 saturation in the fetus: **umbilical vein** (about 80-85%); lowest: **SVC** return.
- Ductus venosus streams oxygenated blood across the **foramen ovale** to the **LV -> coronaries and brain**.
- Fetal PVR **high**, SVR **low** (placenta); the duct shunts **right-to-left**.
- At birth: **↓ PVR, ↑ SVR, LA pressure > RA pressure** -> foramen ovale closes; **↑ PaO2 and ↓ PGE2** -> duct closes.
- **PGE1** opens the duct (duct-dependent lesions; watch for apnoea); **indomethacin/ibuprofen/paracetamol** close it in preterms.
- PVR reaches near-adult levels at about **6-8 weeks** -> large left-to-right shunts present at 4-8 weeks.
- **PFO in about 25%** of adults.
- PPHN: right-to-left shunt, **pre-ductal > post-ductal SpO2**, inhaled NO.
sections.title: High-yield concepts

title: Fetal circulation and the neonatal transition

sections.body:
Before any anatomy, drugs, or ECGs, you must understand the one thing the cardiovascular system is doing. Every disease, every drug, every exam question is a variation on this one theme.

## The cardiovascular system has one job

Strip away everything else and the cardiovascular system has a single purpose: deliver oxygenated blood to tissues that need it, and remove the waste products from those same tissues. Everything in cardiology — every chamber, every valve, every reflex, every drug — exists in service of this one job.

When a tissue does not get enough oxygen, it stops working. The brain stops thinking, the kidney stops filtering, the muscles stop moving, and eventually the heart itself stops contracting. This is why cardiology is the speciality where minutes matter most. A poorly perfused tissue dies in minutes, not hours.

Key concept: Tissue perfusion = the entire purpose of cardiology
Every cardiac problem reduces to one question: is this patient's tissue perfusion adequate, and if not, where in the chain is it breaking down? Master this question and you have a framework for every clinical scenario.

## The three things that must go right

For oxygen to reach a tissue, three things must work in sequence:

1. The pump — the heart must squeeze hard enough and often enough to push blood out
2. The pipes — the vessels must be open, with the right diameter, and able to deliver blood under appropriate pressure
3. The contents — there must be enough blood, and it must carry enough oxygen-bound haemoglobin

Mental model: Think of the cardiovascular system as a sprinkler system in a building. If the pump is broken, no water reaches the sprinklers (cardiac failure). If the pipes are blocked or burst, water cannot reach the right rooms (coronary disease, aortic dissection). If the reservoir is empty, no amount of pumping helps (hypovolaemia). When you assess a patient, you are asking: which of these three is failing right now?

## The two circulations

The cardiovascular system is not one circuit but two, connected in series:

Pulmonary circulation: A low-pressure circuit. The right heart pumps deoxygenated blood through the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and drops off carbon dioxide. Normal pulmonary artery pressure is about 15–30 / 8–12 mmHg, which is roughly one-sixth of systemic pressures. The pulmonary vasculature is thin-walled and not built to handle high pressures.

Systemic circulation: A high-pressure circuit. The left heart pumps oxygenated blood through the body. Normal aortic pressure is roughly 120 / 80 mmHg. The left ventricle is built with thick walls to generate this pressure. The systemic arteries are muscular and can constrict or dilate to control flow.

This pressure asymmetry explains a huge amount of clinical cardiology. The left ventricle is much thicker than the right ventricle. The right ventricle is thin, crescent-shaped, and tolerates volume overload well but pressure overload very poorly. The left ventricle, conversely, handles pressure better than acute volume overload.

Clinical link: This is why a massive pulmonary embolism is so deadly: the thin-walled RV is suddenly asked to generate left-ventricular pressures to push blood past the embolus. It cannot. The RV dilates, fails, and the patient dies of cardiogenic shock from right heart failure — even though the embolus is in the lungs, not the heart.

## The series problem

Because the two circulations are in series (not parallel), the output of the right heart must equal the output of the left heart on average. If the right pumps more than the left, blood backs up in the lungs (pulmonary oedema). If the left pumps more than the right, blood backs up in the systemic veins (peripheral oedema, raised JVP).

Key concept: In series means failure cascades
A problem in one ventricle always eventually causes problems in the other. Left heart failure causes pulmonary congestion, which raises pulmonary pressures, which causes right heart failure. This is why end-stage HF patients have both pulmonary and peripheral oedema — the failure has worked through the system in both directions.

## Two patients, same disease, different presentations

Consider two patients with reduced cardiac output. Both have inadequate tissue perfusion. But the cause of low output determines completely different treatment:

Patient A | Patient B
Cause: Heart muscle is too weak to squeeze (HFrEF, EF 20%) | Cause: Heart cannot fill because the pericardium is compressing it (tamponade)
Problem: The pump itself is broken | Problem: The pump is fine, but it cannot fill
Treatment: Drugs that help the heart contract (dobutamine) or pump less against pressure (vasodilators) | Treatment: Remove the pericardial fluid + give fluids to maintain filling
Diuretics: Help (reduce congestion, reduce wall stress) | Diuretics: Catastrophic (remove the only filling pressure the heart has)

Both patients have low blood pressure. Both have low cardiac output. Both have raised JVP. They look identical at first glance. But the physiological mechanism is opposite — and the treatment that helps patient A will kill patient B.

Exam tip: The single most powerful exam-answering skill is to identify the underlying physiology rather than the surface presentation. When you see 'hypotension + raised JVP + clear lungs', do not immediately reach for diuretics. Ask: why is this happening? Possible answers include tamponade, RV infarction, massive PE, tension pneumothorax — and they all need fluids, not diuresis.

## The hierarchy of cardiology knowledge

By the end of this guide you should be able to put any cardiology fact you learn into one of these levels:

1. Level 1 — Anatomy: What is connected to what (chamber, valve, vessel layouts)
2. Level 2 — Physiology: How things move (electrical conduction, pressure gradients, flow)
3. Level 3 — Pathophysiology: What goes wrong (the mechanism of disease)
4. Level 4 — Pharmacology: How drugs intervene at the physiological level
5. Level 5 — Clinical reasoning: How to put levels 1–4 together at the bedside

Notice that all five levels are required. You cannot understand drug choices without knowing the physiology they manipulate. You cannot understand pathophysiology without knowing what 'normal' looks like. And you cannot read an ECG without knowing what the underlying electrical events actually are.

Checkpoint: Before continuing, ask yourself: what is the single purpose of the cardiovascular system?
To deliver oxygen to tissues that need it. Every cardiac problem is a failure somewhere in this delivery chain. Every drug is a way to fix one of those failure points. If you cannot answer 'why does this matter for tissue perfusion?' for any concept in this guide, you have not yet understood it.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
Blood pressure is not generated by the heart alone. It is the product of cardiac output and vascular resistance. This single relationship explains every type of shock, every antihypertensive, and every emergency intervention.

## The equation

Equation: Blood pressure (BP) = Cardiac output (CO) × Systemic vascular resistance (SVR)

Or in haemodynamic terms, applied to the systemic circulation:

Equation: MAP − CVP = CO × SVR

where MAP is mean arterial pressure and CVP is central venous pressure. Since CVP is normally small relative to MAP, we usually simplify to BP = CO × SVR.

This is the cardiovascular version of Ohm's law (voltage = current × resistance). It is the most important equation in haemodynamics, because it tells you the two and only two ways blood pressure can be low: low cardiac output, or low resistance, or both.

Key concept: Hypotension has only two possible causes: low CO or low SVR
When you see a hypotensive patient, your first question is: is the cardiac output low or is the resistance low? The answer determines treatment. Low CO → identify why (preload, contractility, obstruction). Low SVR → identify why (sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic, drug-induced). This is the single most useful clinical reasoning tool in emergency cardiology.

## The two pathways to shock

Type of shock | CO | SVR | Clinical hallmark
Cardiogenic | ↓ (the heart cannot pump) | ↑ (compensatory) | Cold, clammy, mottled extremities; low CO causes vasoconstriction
Hypovolaemic | ↓ (no blood to pump) | ↑ (compensatory) | Cold extremities, flat JVP, dry mucous membranes
Obstructive (tamponade, PE, tension PTX) | ↓ (filling or output blocked) | ↑ (compensatory) | Cold + raised JVP (preload cannot be used)
Distributive (sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic) | ↑ or normal (early) | ↓ (vasodilation) | Warm, vasodilated, bounding pulses (early); cold later as CO fails

Clinical link: Why "warm shock vs cold shock" matters at the bedside: The first physical examination finding in a hypotensive patient — temperature of extremities, capillary refill — tells you whether SVR is high or low. Cold extremities = high SVR = the heart is the problem or there is hypovolaemia. Warm extremities = low SVR = distributive shock (sepsis until proven otherwise). This single observation determines whether you reach for inotropes (cardiogenic) or vasopressors (distributive).

## Vasopressors vs inotropes

This distinction is one of the most clinically important in critical care:

- Vasopressors increase SVR — they constrict arterioles. The main vasopressor is norepinephrine (α1 agonist primarily). Vasopressin (V1 receptor agonist), phenylephrine (pure α1), and high-dose dopamine are other examples.
- Inotropes increase contractility — they make the heart squeeze harder. The main inotrope is dobutamine (β1 agonist). Milrinone (PDE3 inhibitor) and epinephrine (mixed) are alternatives.

The rule of thumb:

- Distributive shock (low SVR): start with a vasopressor — norepinephrine.
- Cardiogenic shock (low CO): start with an inotrope — dobutamine. Add norepinephrine if MAP still inadequate.
- Mixed cardiogenic and distributive (often in septic cardiomyopathy or end-stage HF with sepsis): combine norepinephrine and dobutamine.

Key concept: Norepinephrine is the modern first-line vasopressor for nearly all shock
The SOAP II trial established norepinephrine as superior to dopamine in cardiogenic shock (fewer arrhythmias, trend to lower mortality). It is also first-line in septic shock (Surviving Sepsis guidelines). "Levophed" is no longer the drug of last resort — it is the modern default. Memorise this — it is a frequent exam answer.

## Mean arterial pressure — the perfusion number

Systolic blood pressure is what gets quoted, but the more physiologically important number is mean arterial pressure (MAP) — the average pressure driving perfusion over the cardiac cycle.

Equation: MAP ≈ (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3
or MAP ≈ DBP + (Pulse pressure / 3)

Why is the diastolic pressure weighted more heavily? Because most of the cardiac cycle is spent in diastole. The brain and other organs perfuse based on the time-weighted average pressure.

For most organs, perfusion is maintained as long as MAP is >65 mmHg. Below this:

- The kidney loses its ability to autoregulate → falling GFR → AKI
- The brain loses cerebral autoregulation (or, in chronic hypertensives, it has been reset to a higher threshold)
- The coronaries themselves get less diastolic perfusion

This is why MAP >65 mmHg is the target in nearly all shock states.

## The hypertensive emergency exception

The 25% MAP rule for hypertensive emergencies is a direct application of Ohm's law plus the concept of autoregulation reset:

A patient with chronic hypertension has structurally adapted vasculature (medial hypertrophy of arterioles). Cerebral autoregulation, normally working between MAP 60–150 mmHg, is shifted rightward — perhaps to 80–180 mmHg. The brain is now underperfused at "normal" blood pressures.

If a chronic hypertensive presents with BP 240/130 (MAP 167), and you rapidly drop the MAP to 100 mmHg, you are below their shifted lower autoregulation limit. Result: watershed cerebral ischaemia, ischaemic stroke. The 25% rule limits the drop to one that the cerebral vessels can compensate for.

Exam tip: Memorise the 25% rule with the actual math. If MAP is 160, the maximum reduction in the first hour is 40 mmHg (25%) → target MAP 120. If MAP is 200, the maximum reduction is 50 → target MAP 150. If you see an option that brings BP to 120/80 in the first hour for a chronic hypertensive in emergency, it is wrong — that is the trap. Slow, controlled reduction is correct.

## Pulse pressure — the often-ignored signal

Pulse pressure = SBP − DBP. Normal is 40–60 mmHg.

- Narrow pulse pressure (<25% of SBP, e.g., 95/80) → low stroke volume (HFrEF, cardiogenic shock, severe AS, tamponade)
- Wide pulse pressure (e.g., 160/50) → high stroke volume or rapid diastolic runoff. Causes: aortic regurgitation (the most classic), AV fistula, PDA, thyrotoxicosis, anaemia, hyperdynamic states, isolated systolic hypertension in elderly (stiff aorta)

Key concept: Pulse pressure is a "free" haemodynamic clue
Look at BP: 160/50 with the bounding pulse of someone with severe AR. Look at BP: 88/72 with the thready pulse of cardiogenic shock. Pulse pressure tells you about stroke volume without needing any equipment. A patient with a pulse pressure <25% of their SBP is likely in low-output failure.

Checkpoint: A patient has BP 80/65, raised JVP, cold extremities, lungs clear. Using Ohm's law and your knowledge of preload, what are the most likely diagnoses?
Cold extremities = high SVR (so this is not distributive shock). Raised JVP = high right-sided filling pressures. Clear lungs = no LV congestion. So we have low CO with high preload available but not being used. The classic differential is obstructive shock: Cardiac tamponade (pericardial compression)
Tension pneumothorax
Massive pulmonary embolism
RV infarction
All four need fluids (preload-dependent), not diuresis. All four need a specific intervention to remove the obstruction (pericardiocentesis, chest decompression, thrombolysis, reperfusion). The pattern "shock + raised JVP + clear lungs" is one of the most useful pattern-recognitions in emergency medicine.

sections.body:
The ECG is a record of cardiac electrical activity projected onto the surface of the body. Every wave, every interval, every deflection represents a specific electrical event. Master what each one means and you stop memorising patterns — you reason through them.

## What you are actually looking at

The ECG records voltage changes between electrodes placed on the body. When a wave of depolarisation moves toward an electrode, the deflection is positive (upward). When it moves away, the deflection is negative (downward). When the wave is perpendicular to the electrode, the deflection is small or biphasic.

This is the single most important conceptual fact about ECGs: the ECG is a vector. It tells you the direction and magnitude of electrical movement. Once you internalise this, you can reason out axis, BBB, infarction localisation, and chamber enlargement from first principles.

Key concept: The 12 leads are 12 cameras pointing at the heart from different angles
Each lead shows the heart's electrical activity from one viewing angle. Lead II looks up from below (inferior view). Lead V1 looks at the heart from the right side. Lead V6 looks from the left side. When you see a change in a lead, you are seeing it from that specific angle — which tells you where in the heart the change is happening.

## The waves — and what each one represents

Wave / interval | Electrical event | Normal value
P wave | Atrial depolarisation (SA node fires → spreads across atria) | <120 ms, <2.5 mm tall
PR interval | Time from atrial depolarisation start to ventricular depolarisation start. Mostly AV node delay. | 120–200 ms (3–5 small squares)
QRS complex | Ventricular depolarisation. Q = septal depolarisation (left to right), R = main LV mass, S = late LV/posterior | <120 ms (<3 small squares)
ST segment | Plateau phase of ventricular action potential. Should be isoelectric (on the baseline). | No deviation >1 mm (limb), >2 mm (precordial)
T wave | Ventricular repolarisation | Same direction as QRS in most leads
QT interval | Total duration of ventricular electrical activity (depolarisation + repolarisation) | QTc <440 ms men, <460 ms women
U wave | Possible Purkinje repolarisation. Often invisible. Prominent in hypokalaemia. | Small, often absent

Clinical link: Why each interval matters clinically: PR >200 ms = first-degree AV block. PR progressively lengthens then drops = Mobitz I (Wenckebach). Fixed PR with dropped beats = Mobitz II.
QRS >120 ms = bundle branch block (look at V1: RBBB has rSR' pattern, LBBB has wide monophasic R). Wide QRS in tachycardia raises concern for VT.
ST elevation in 2+ contiguous leads = STEMI. Concave-up ST elevation in many leads = pericarditis.
QTc >500 ms = high risk for torsades. Drug-induced or congenital.

## The systematic approach — read every ECG the same way

The single best way to avoid missing findings is to read every ECG in the same order, every time. The order does not matter much — the consistency does.

1. Rate — count R-R intervals. 1500/small squares between R waves, or 300/large squares.
2. Rhythm — is it sinus? P before every QRS, QRS after every P, regular?
3. Axis — look at leads I and aVF. Normal axis: both positive. Left axis: I positive, aVF negative. Right axis: I negative, aVF positive.
4. Intervals — PR, QRS, QTc.
5. Morphology — atria — P wave shape (P-pulmonale = tall P in II = RA enlargement; P-mitrale = wide notched P in II = LA enlargement).
6. Morphology — ventricles — Q waves (pathological if >1 mm wide or >25% of R height), ST segment, T wave, U wave.
7. Compare to old ECG if available. A subtle change against a baseline is often more important than the absolute appearance.

## Lead orientation — territory recognition

The 12 leads of an ECG group naturally by territory:

Leads | Territory | Artery
II, III, aVF | Inferior wall | RCA (85%) or LCx (15%)
V1, V2 | Septum | LAD (proximal)
V3, V4 | Anterior wall | LAD
V5, V6, I, aVL | Lateral wall | LCx or diagonal of LAD
V7–V9 (posterior) | Posterior wall | RCA (right-dominant) or LCx
V4R (right-sided) | RV | Proximal RCA
aVR | Cavity / right shoulder | Diffuse subendocardial / left main

Key concept: ST elevation in aVR is the most underdiagnosed STEMI equivalent
ST elevation in aVR ≥1 mm + diffuse ST depression elsewhere = left main or proximal LAD occlusion. This pattern is missed because aVR is often ignored. Mortality is very high if not recognised quickly — these patients need urgent angiography. Always look at aVR. If it is elevated more than V1 with diffuse depression, treat as STEMI equivalent.

## The four "must recognise instantly" patterns

These ECG patterns are immediate clinical actions. You cannot afford to miss them or delay.

1. STEMI — ST elevation ≥1 mm in 2 contiguous limb leads or ≥2 mm in V2–V3 (≥1.5 mm in women). Activates the cath lab.
2. Complete heart block — P waves and QRS complexes dissociated, regular bradycardia at 30–40 bpm. Needs pacing.
3. Sustained VT — wide complex tachycardia, regular, monomorphic. Needs cardioversion (if unstable) or amiodarone/lidocaine. Treat wide complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise.
4. Torsades de pointes — polymorphic wide complex tachycardia with QRS twisting around baseline + long QT. Needs IV magnesium 2 g; do not use amiodarone (further prolongs QT).

## STEMI patterns by anatomy

Knowing which leads show ST elevation tells you which artery is occluded, which territory is at risk, and what complications to anticipate.

Pattern | Likely vessel | Specific things to look for
ST↑ in II, III, aVF | RCA (typically) | Check V4R for RV involvement. Check for AV block (RCA supplies AV node).
ST↑ in II, III, aVF + III > II | RCA (proximal) | Highly suggests RCA over LCx
ST↑ in II, III, aVF + I & aVL negative | RCA | 
ST↑ in II, III, aVF + I & aVL ST↑ also | LCx (left-dominant) | 
ST↑ in V1–V4 | LAD (anterior) | Watch for cardiogenic shock if proximal — large territory
ST↑ in V1–V6 + I + aVL | Proximal LAD before first septal/diagonal | "Widow-maker" pattern — high mortality
ST↑ in aVR > V1 + diffuse ST↓ | Left main or 3-vessel disease | Urgent angiography. Possibly CABG rather than PCI.
ST↓ in V1–V3 with tall R waves (mirror image) | Posterior MI — RCA or LCx | Get posterior leads (V7–V9). Often missed.

Exam tip: Wellens' syndrome: Biphasic or deeply inverted T waves in V2–V3 in a patient with recent chest pain (now pain-free, near-normal troponin). This represents a critical proximal LAD stenosis that has not yet infarcted. These patients look stable but are about to have a massive anterior MI if not catheterised urgently. Recognising this saves anterior wall.

## The ECG "negatives" — what abnormalities also tell you

- Low voltage QRS (<5 mm in limb leads, <10 mm in precordial) → consider: pericardial effusion (causes electrical attenuation), obesity, severe COPD, infiltrative cardiomyopathy (amyloid).
- Electrical alternans (alternating QRS amplitudes) → large pericardial effusion with the heart "swinging" inside it. Pathognomonic for tamponade physiology.
- Low voltage + poor R wave progression + apparent LVH (paradox: ECG looks low voltage but echo shows hypertrophy) → think cardiac amyloid. This "discordance between ECG and echo" is highly characteristic.
- Tall peaked T waves → hyperkalaemia (early). Progression: peaked T → PR prolongation → QRS widening → sine wave → asystole.
- Flat T waves with U waves → hypokalaemia.
- Short QT → hypercalcaemia, digoxin effect (scooped ST), congenital short QT.

Checkpoint: A 65-year-old man with chest pain has ST elevation in II, III, aVF. He becomes profoundly hypotensive after sublingual nitrate. What happened, and which lead would have predicted this disaster?
Inferior STEMI involves the RV in 30–50% of cases. RV infarction is preload-dependent — the only way the infarcted RV can produce forward flow is high venous filling pressure pushing through it. Nitrates cause venodilation → preload crash → RV cannot fill → systemic hypotension and arrest. The lead that would have predicted this is V4R (right-sided V4): ST elevation ≥1 mm in V4R is diagnostic of RV infarction. Every inferior STEMI deserves V4R before nitrates.

sections.body:
The cardiovascular system is regulated by an overlapping web of nervous and hormonal signals. In heart failure, these signals — designed for acute survival — become chronic enemies. Understanding them explains why GDMT works and why "more is better" is wrong.

## The body's three main cardiovascular control systems

1. The autonomic nervous system — sympathetic (fast, "fight or flight") and parasympathetic (slow, "rest and digest")
2. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) — slower, hormonal, regulates volume and pressure over hours to days
3. The natriuretic peptide system — counter-regulatory; "release valve" against fluid overload

These three systems normally balance each other. In disease — especially heart failure — the balance breaks. Sympathetic and RAAS activation become chronic and pathological. Natriuretic peptide effects become inadequate. Almost all heart failure pharmacology aims to restore this balance.

Key concept: The "neurohormonal theory" of heart failure is the defining insight of modern cardiology
From the 1980s onward, evidence showed that chronic neurohormonal activation — not pump failure itself — drives disease progression in HFrEF. Drugs that block this activation (ACEi, ARNI, BB, MRA) improve mortality. Drugs that simply boost pump function (positive inotropes, milrinone) worsen mortality. The pump is not the only problem — the signalling is.

## The sympathetic nervous system — acute friend, chronic enemy

The sympathetic nervous system is the body's emergency response. In acute hypotension, it activates within seconds:

- Heart: β1 stimulation → ↑HR, ↑contractility → ↑CO
- Arterioles: α1 stimulation → vasoconstriction → ↑SVR → ↑BP
- Veins: α1 stimulation → venoconstriction → ↑preload
- Adrenal medulla: releases epinephrine into bloodstream
- Kidney: β1 stimulation of juxtaglomerular cells → renin release (triggers RAAS)

This is brilliant for surviving acute blood loss. But in chronic HFrEF, the body is in a state of "permanent emergency" — sympathetic tone is constantly elevated. Norepinephrine levels are 2–5× normal. The consequences are devastating:

- Direct cardiomyocyte toxicity (catecholamine cardiomyopathy)
- β-receptor downregulation → the heart loses its ability to respond to its own signals
- Increased myocardial O₂ demand → demand ischaemia → further damage
- Adverse cardiac remodelling (apoptosis, fibrosis, hypertrophy)
- Pro-arrhythmic state → sudden cardiac death

Clinical link: This explains why beta-blockers — drugs that "weaken the heart" — improve heart failure mortality. By blocking chronic sympathetic over-activation, they protect cardiomyocytes from toxicity, allow β-receptors to re-sensitise, and reduce ventricular wall stress. Over months, the heart recovers function. The drug that depresses contractility acutely allows contractility to recover chronically. This is the central paradox of HF pharmacotherapy.

## The RAAS axis in detail

RAAS is a multi-step cascade that regulates blood pressure and sodium balance:

1. Trigger: Low renal perfusion (or β1 stimulation, or low Na delivery to macula densa) → juxtaglomerular cells release renin.
2. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen (made by the liver) → angiotensin I.
3. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), predominantly in the lung endothelium, converts angiotensin I → angiotensin II (the active hormone).
4. Angiotensin II does several things:
  - Potent vasoconstrictor (acts on AT1 receptors) → ↑SVR → ↑BP
  - Stimulates aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex
  - Stimulates ADH release → water retention
  - Acts directly on the brain → thirst
  - Promotes cardiac and vascular fibrosis (long-term remodelling)
5. Aldosterone acts on the distal nephron → reabsorbs Na (and therefore water) → ↑intravascular volume → ↑preload → ↑BP. Also promotes K excretion (low K when high aldosterone).

Diagram: The RAAS axis and the drugs that block each step (drawing not carried over)

## The natriuretic peptide system — the counter-regulator

While RAAS retains volume and raises pressure, the natriuretic peptide system does the opposite — promotes natriuresis (sodium loss), vasodilation, and inhibits RAAS.

- ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) — released by atrial myocytes in response to stretch (high filling pressures).
- BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide) — released by ventricular myocytes in response to stretch.
- NT-proBNP — the inactive cleavage product. Longer half-life, easier to measure.

These peptides are degraded by neprilysin. So if you inhibit neprilysin, you augment natriuretic peptide activity — which is the mechanism of sacubitril (the "S" in ARNI / sacubitril-valsartan).

Key concept: BNP/NT-proBNP is a marker of cardiac wall stretch — not just HF
BNP rises any time atrial or ventricular myocytes are stretched: HF, MI, pulmonary embolism, atrial fibrillation, severe sepsis. It is sensitive but not specific. Low BNP <100 in a dyspnoeic patient makes HF very unlikely (high negative predictive value). High BNP confirms cardiac stress but not its cause. BNP can be falsely LOW in obese patients (adipose tissue clears it) and in flash pulmonary oedema (not enough time for myocytes to synthesise and release peptide).

## How GDMT targets all three systems simultaneously

The four pillars of HFrEF GDMT each block a different node of the neurohormonal axis:

Pillar | What it blocks | Net effect
ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) | Angiotensin II (via valsartan) + augments natriuretic peptides (via sacubitril) | ↓ vasoconstriction, ↓ aldosterone, ↑ natriuresis
Beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) | Sympathetic activation at β1 | ↓ HR, ↓ contractility (acute), allow remodelling (chronic)
MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) | Aldosterone at mineralocorticoid receptor | ↓ fibrosis, ↓ Na retention, ↑ K retention
SGLT2i (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) | Multiple — direct cardiac effects, natriuresis, reduced sympathetic tone, metabolic shift | ↓ preload, ↓ afterload, improved energetics

Clinical link: Why all four pillars together work better than any one alone: Each pillar leaves "escape routes" that the others close. ACEi alone leaves aldosterone escape (chronic ACEi use has been associated with rising aldosterone over time) — MRA closes that escape. BB alone leaves RAAS unblocked. SGLT2i works through pathways the others do not touch. The synergy is mathematical, not just additive — the relative risk reductions multiply. A patient on all four pillars has ~70% lower mortality than baseline; on three pillars, ~50%; on two, ~30%. Every missing pillar is mortality unsaved.

## The HFpEF problem

For decades, the neurohormonal model worked beautifully for HFrEF but poorly for HFpEF. Trials of ACEi (PEP-CHF), ARBs (CHARM-Preserved, I-PRESERVE), BBs (SENIORS), MRAs (TOPCAT) in HFpEF showed disappointing results.

The breakthrough was SGLT2 inhibitors. EMPEROR-Preserved (empagliflozin) and DELIVER (dapagliflozin) both showed mortality and hospitalisation benefit across the full EF spectrum, including HFpEF. SGLT2i is the first drug class to clearly improve outcomes in HFpEF.

Exam tip: The current state of HFpEF treatment (high yield): SGLT2i — first-line, Class I recommendation
Diuretics — for congestion symptoms
Treat comorbidities — HTN, AF, obesity, DM, OSA
MRA — Class IIb (TOPCAT — heterogeneous results, possible signal in Americas)
ARNI — Class IIb (PARAGON-HF — borderline benefit in lower-EF HFpEF, women)
The HFpEF treatment hierarchy is fundamentally different from HFrEF — do not assume the four pillars apply equally.

Checkpoint: A 70-year-old HFrEF patient (EF 30%) on ramipril 10 mg, metoprolol succinate 200 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, and dapagliflozin 10 mg. NT-proBNP is 800 pg/mL (down from 3500 six months ago). What is happening physiologically, and what should you do next?
Falling NT-proBNP reflects reduced wall stretch — meaning filling pressures are dropping and the ventricle is geometrically improving. This is reverse remodelling in action: the four pillars are working. The neurohormonal blockade has reduced cardiac afterload and preload, allowing the dilated heart to shrink toward normal. Next steps: consider switching ramipril to sacubitril/valsartan (PARADIGM-HF showed superior outcomes vs ACEi). If switching, hold ramipril for 36 hours before starting ARNI to avoid angioedema. Re-check labs in 1–2 weeks. Repeat echo at 6 months — many patients on full GDMT show EF improvement (sometimes back to >50%) and stable BNP.

sections.body:
The heart is the one organ that perfuses itself. The rules governing coronary blood flow are unique — and understanding them explains why tachycardia is ischaemic, why the subendocardium is the most vulnerable zone, and why certain drugs save the myocardium and others accelerate its death.

## The fundamental peculiarity of coronary perfusion

Every other organ in the body receives most of its blood flow during systole, when cardiac output is highest and arteries are being pushed open by high pressure. The heart is different. The left ventricle receives approximately 85% of its coronary blood flow during diastole.

Why? Because during systole, the LV myocardium contracts so forcefully that it compresses the intramyocardial coronary vessels from within, particularly in the subendocardium. The squeezing muscle literally collapses its own blood supply during the contraction phase. Only when the muscle relaxes in diastole do the vessels open up and fill.

Key concept: Coronary perfusion pressure = Aortic diastolic pressure − LVEDP
Blood flows into the coronary bed during diastole, driven by the aortic diastolic pressure (the pressure still in the aorta when the aortic valve is closed). It is resisted by the downstream pressure in the relaxed LV (LVEDP). So: CPP = DBP − LVEDP. Both can be manipulated: DBP falls in aortic regurgitation (diastolic blood pressure is low) and in tachycardia (less diastolic time means less diastolic fill of the aorta). LVEDP rises in HF, LVH, and ischaemia.

## Why tachycardia is profoundly ischaemic

As heart rate rises, both components of coronary perfusion are simultaneously worsened:

- Supply falls: diastole shortens → less time for coronary filling. At HR 75, diastole is ~0.5 s. At HR 150, diastole is ~0.2 s.
- Demand rises: each systole produces more wall stress and more oxygen consumption, and the heart is doing this more times per minute.

This double whammy — less supply, more demand — is the mechanism of every exertional angina episode. The coronary blood flow simply cannot keep up with the oxygen demand at high heart rates, particularly if there is a fixed obstruction that limits the maximum achievable flow.

Clinical link: This is the physiological basis of the exercise treadmill test. Exercise increases HR and contractility → O₂ demand rises → if a coronary stenosis is present, the vessel cannot dilate enough to meet demand → ischaemia develops → ST changes, chest pain. The test identifies the heart rate at which supply-demand mismatch occurs. A patient who develops ST depression at low workload (HR <120, Stage 2 Bruce) has a very critical lesion — close to failure at rest.

## Coronary autoregulation

Over a wide range of perfusion pressures (roughly MAP 60–130 mmHg), the coronary vessels autoregulate — they dilate or constrict to maintain relatively constant coronary blood flow despite changes in perfusion pressure. This is mediated primarily by metabolic factors (adenosine, CO₂, lactate, H⁺ — all byproducts of myocardial activity, which act as local vasodilators).

The clinical implication: within the autoregulatory range, coronary flow is demand-driven, not pressure-driven. The heart takes what it needs.

But autoregulation has limits:

- Below MAP ~60 mmHg — the coronary vessels are maximally dilated and can no longer compensate for pressure drops. Flow becomes pressure-dependent. Ischaemia occurs.
- In the presence of a significant stenosis — the vessels distal to the stenosis are chronically vasodilated (already using their autoregulatory reserve just to maintain baseline flow). There is no further reserve. Any increase in demand or further fall in perfusion pressure causes ischaemia.

Key concept: Coronary reserve = the difference between resting flow and maximum flow
In a normal coronary artery, maximum vasodilation can increase flow 4–5 times above resting. This reserve allows demand to rise substantially during exercise without ischaemia. A 70% stenosis leaves very little reserve — resting flow may be maintained but there is almost no ability to increase. A 90% stenosis: resting flow is impaired, reserve is essentially zero. Fractional flow reserve (FFR) measures this reserve directly — FFR <0.80 indicates a haemodynamically significant stenosis warranting intervention.

## The subendocardium — the most vulnerable zone

Not all myocardium is equally at risk of ischaemia. The subendocardium (the inner layer of the LV wall, adjacent to the cavity) is the first to become ischaemic and the last to be rescued, for several reasons:

1. Higher wall stress — by Laplace's law, the inner layers of the wall carry more tension than the outer layers (the radius at the endocardium is larger relative to where the tension acts).
2. Longest oxygen diffusion path from epicardial coronaries — coronary arteries run on the outside (epicardium) and penetrate inward. The subendocardium is furthest from the supply.
3. Highest intramyocardial compression during systole — the systolic squeeze compresses the intramural vessels maximally at the endocardium.
4. Already maximally vasodilated — due to high metabolic demand, the subendocardial vessels have less autoregulatory reserve.

Clinical link: This explains the ECG pattern of subendocardial ischaemia: Diffuse horizontal or downsloping ST depression in many leads (not elevation) — because the ischaemic zone is the inner layer of the LV, not a transmural zone. Classic examples: NSTEMI, demand ischaemia, hypertrophic LV with fixed LAD stenosis during exertion. Compare this to transmural ischaemia (STEMI), where the full thickness of the wall is infarcted and ECG shows ST elevation in the affected territory.

## Coronary steal

Coronary steal is a paradoxical phenomenon where a vasodilator that should increase coronary flow actually reduces flow to ischaemic zones.

It occurs when a vasodilator selectively dilates the normal coronary vasculature (which still has reserve), drawing blood away from the ischaemic zone (which is already maximally dilated and cannot dilate further). Blood "steals" from the territory that needs it most to the territory that needs it least.

Key concept: Dipyridamole and adenosine cause coronary steal — which is why they are used in stress testing
In pharmacological stress testing (for patients who cannot exercise), adenosine or regadenoson (adenosine receptor agonist) is infused to maximally vasodilate the coronary vasculature. Zones supplied by stenotic arteries (already maximally dilated) cannot increase flow further — so they appear as perfusion defects on nuclear imaging or echo. Dipyridamole works by blocking adenosine reuptake (raising endogenous adenosine). The "stress" is the steal, not exercise.

## Collateral circulation

In chronic obstructive coronary disease, the heart develops collateral vessels — small bridging arteries that connect branches of different coronary territories. They are essentially natural bypass grafts.

Collaterals develop slowly, over weeks to months, in response to chronic ischaemia. They are not present acutely. This is why:

- A patient with a chronic total occlusion (CTO) of the RCA, fed by collaterals from the LAD, may have a near-normal resting ECG and minimal symptoms — the collaterals are doing the work.
- The same patient who acutely occludes an LAD (first MI, no prior disease) dies rapidly — there are no collaterals to protect the anterior wall.
- Patients with prior MI who later have a second MI in the same territory may have less damage because collaterals from the infarct territory have been growing since the first event.

Exam tip: The "protection by chronic disease" paradox: Patients with multivessel CAD who have a STEMI may survive it better than patients with a first-ever event in a "virgin" artery — because collaterals have grown. An examiner who presents a chronic stable patient with a totally occluded RCA but a good RV function and minimal inferior wall scar is testing whether you understand collateral protection. Treat what is haemodynamically significant, not what is anatomically dramatic.

## Myocardial oxygen supply and demand — the master table

 | Increases O₂ demand | Decreases O₂ demand
HR | ↑ HR (exercise, AF, tachyarrhythmia) | ↓ HR (beta-blockers, rate control)
Contractility | ↑ (inotropes, sympathetic activation) | ↓ (beta-blockers)
Wall stress (preload × radius or afterload × thickness) | ↑ preload, ↑ afterload, LV dilation | ↓ afterload (vasodilators), ↓ preload (nitrates, diuretics), hypertrophy then reverse remodelling
Diastolic perfusion time | ↑ HR (shortens diastole) | ↓ HR (lengthens diastole)
Coronary perfusion pressure | ↓ DBP (AR, tachycardia), ↑ LVEDP | ↑ DBP (vasopressors), ↓ LVEDP (diuretics)

Checkpoint: A patient with known 3-vessel CAD develops acute chest pain during a dentist appointment (high anxiety). HR is 130, BP 185/95. His GTN spray was left at home. What drug class would most efficiently relieve his ischaemia and why?
The ischaemia is driven by sympathetic activation causing high HR (reduces diastolic perfusion time, increases O₂ demand) and high BP (increases afterload and wall stress). The ideal drug reduces both simultaneously: IV metoprolol (beta-blocker). It slows HR (restores diastolic coronary fill time, reduces O₂ demand) and modestly reduces BP. A single IV dose of 2.5–5 mg metoprolol is first-line for rate-related ischaemia. GTN would also help by reducing preload and some afterload — but without GTN present, IV BB is the correct answer. Avoid pure vasodilators that might reflex tachycardia (e.g., IV hydralazine alone would increase HR, worsening ischaemia).
