sections.body:
Each valvular lesion generates a constellation of signs that, taken together, are more specific than any individual finding. Knowing the full sign set for each valve lesion — from the inspection of the hands to the character of the last Korotkoff sound — is the hallmark of the complete cardiovascular clinician.

## Aortic stenosis (AS) — the complete examination

Examination component | Sign in severe AS | Mechanism
Pulse | Slow-rising, plateau pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) | Narrowed valve limits ejection velocity
Pulse pressure | Narrow pulse pressure (<40 mmHg) | Reduced stroke volume through stenotic valve
Apex beat | Sustained, heaving (pressure-loaded) | LV hypertrophy from chronic pressure overload
Thrill | Systolic thrill at RUSB and carotids in severe AS | High-velocity turbulent jet
S1 | Normal or soft (if long PR interval) | Usually unaffected
S2 | Soft or absent A2; paradoxical splitting in severe AS | Calcified immobile AV; delayed LV emptying → A2 comes after P2
S4 | Prominent S4 gallop at the apex | Forceful atrial kick against hypertrophied, stiff LV
Murmur | Harsh, crescendo-decrescendo ESM at RUSB, radiates to carotids | Turbulent flow through stenotic AV orifice
Severity clues | Later peak of murmur; longer duration; softer A2; paradoxical split S2 — all suggest greater severity | Higher gradient → later peak; stiffer valve → less A2

## Aortic regurgitation (AR) — the peripheral signs

AR generates dramatic peripheral findings from the combination of high stroke volume (↑ systolic pressure) and rapid diastolic runoff (↓ diastolic pressure) → wide pulse pressure + collapsing pulse:

Sign | Technique | Mechanism
Corrigan's pulse | Visible prominent carotid pulsation in the neck | Large stroke volume → forceful carotid distension
de Musset's sign | Head nodding rhythmically with each heartbeat | Large stroke volume → head moves with each cardiac cycle
Quincke's sign | Visible capillary pulsation in the nail bed when gentle pressure applied to the fingertip | Wide pulse pressure transmitted to capillary bed — alternating blanching and flushing
Duroziez's sign | Place the stethoscope over the femoral artery and apply partial occlusive pressure proximally → a systolic murmur is normal; with AR → an additional diastolic murmur appears (to-and-fro murmur) | Diastolic retrograde flow in the femoral artery from the wide pulse pressure
Traube's sign | "Pistol shot" sounds heard over the femoral artery with the stethoscope placed on the artery without pressure | The large arterial pulse against the artery wall creates an audible "shot"
Hill's sign | Popliteal SBP >20 mmHg more than brachial SBP (normal: popliteal is only 10–20 mmHg more) | Wave amplification of the collapsing pulse in the lower limb arteries; indicates severe AR

## Mitral stenosis (MS) — the complete examination

- Malar flush: bilateral high cheekbone reddish-violaceous flush — ↓ CO + ↑ venodilation from pulmonary hypertension
- Pulse: small volume, may be irregularly irregular (AF — very common in MS); if in sinus rhythm, a normal rate pulse
- JVP: elevated if pulmonary hypertension has caused RV failure; prominent a wave if sinus rhythm + RV hypertrophy from PH
- Apex: tapping (palpable loud S1) — not displaced (unless there is also MR); parasternal heave if RV enlargement from PH
- Auscultation: loud S1 → opening snap → mid-diastolic low-pitched rumble (presystolic accentuation in SR) → loud P2 if pulmonary hypertension → Graham Steell murmur if severe PH
- Severity indicators: shorter S2-OS interval → more severe; longer diastolic rumble → more severe; absent OS (heavily calcified MV) → severe but calcified

## Mitral regurgitation (MR) — the complete examination

- Pulse: hyperdynamic (large volume), regular or AF in chronic MR
- Apex: displaced laterally and inferiorly (volume-loaded LV dilation); hyperdynamic/thrusting character
- S1: soft or absent (MV leaflets cannot close properly — low-energy closure)
- S3: common in significant MR (large diastolic filling from the regurgitant volume returning from the LA)
- Murmur: pansystolic, blowing, high-pitched, best at apex, radiates to left axilla (posterior leaflet MR) or LUSB (anterior leaflet MR or chordal rupture)
- Acute severe MR (papillary muscle rupture post-MI): murmur may be SHORT (not pansystolic) — the acutely non-compliant LA rapidly equalises pressure with the LV → the pressure gradient driving regurgitation disappears before S2. The hyperdynamic EF on echo (ejecting into low-resistance LA) is a clue.

title: Valvular heart disease — the complete sign set

sections.body:
Congenital heart disease in adults and children presents with a characteristic examination pattern for each lesion. The combination of cyanosis (or its absence), splitting of S2, the character of murmurs, and the pattern of heaves and pulses — assembled systematically — points to the correct anatomical diagnosis before any imaging is performed.

## Atrial septal defect (ASD)

Sign | Finding | Mechanism
Cyanosis | Absent (left-to-right shunt — oxygenated blood flows right) | LA→RA → ↑ pulmonary blood flow → fully oxygenated blood in systemic circulation
Pulse | Normal or small volume | Small-to-moderate shunt: normal systemic CO
Apex | Normal or mildly hyperdynamic | Mild LV volume loading from increased pulmonary venous return
Parasternal heave | Present — RV volume overload from shunt | RV handles ↑ volume → ↑ RV size → heave
S2 | Fixed wide splitting — the DIAGNOSTIC sign | The atrial-level communication equalises RA pressure between inspiration and expiration → P2 delay is fixed regardless of breathing
Murmur | Ejection systolic murmur at LUSB (pulmonary flow murmur — from ↑ flow across the PV, NOT from the ASD itself) | Increased pulmonary blood flow → relative PS
Diastolic | Mid-diastolic tricuspid flow murmur at LLSB (if Qp:Qs >2:1) | Increased TV flow from extra RA volume

## Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

- Murmur: harsh, loud pansystolic murmur at the LLSB (3rd–4th left ICS). Thrill almost always palpable. Grade 4–5/6 in moderate VSD. "Maladie de Roger" — a small VSD with a very loud murmur (Vin ordinaire with much turbulence through a tiny hole).
- S2: normal splitting (unless pulmonary hypertension develops — then P2 becomes loud; in Eisenmenger: single or reversed splitting)
- Apex: hyperdynamic (LV volume overload from pulmonary-to-systemic recirculation)
- Cyanosis: absent initially (L-R shunt); with Eisenmenger → central cyanosis + loud P2 + murmur shortens/disappears

## Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)

- Pulse: collapsing/bounding (wide pulse pressure — similar to AR, from diastolic runoff into the pulmonary circuit)
- Murmur: continuous "machinery" (Gibson) murmur — occupies all of systole and all of diastole; best heard at the left infraclavicular area or upper left sternal border; a thrill may be palpable
- Differential cyanosis: in Eisenmenger PDA — cyanosis in the lower limbs only (right-to-left ductal shunting → deoxygenated blood enters the descending aorta below the subclavian arteries → lower limb cyanosis; upper limbs receive oxygenated blood from the aortic arch above the duct)

## Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

- Central cyanosis + clubbing: from birth or early life; degree of cyanosis correlates with severity of right ventricular outflow obstruction
- Parasternal heave: RV hypertrophy (infundibular hypertrophy in TOF)
- S2: single (P2 is soft or absent — reduced pulmonary blood flow → soft pulmonic component)
- Murmur: ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal border (from the RVOTO/PS component — NOT from the VSD which is non-restrictive). With increasing obstruction → louder and longer RVOTO murmur initially, but in severe obstruction → less blood can get through → murmur shortens (less flow = less turbulence). During a tet spell: the murmur becomes very soft or disappears (RVOTO is so severe that little blood reaches the pulmonary artery).

## Eisenmenger syndrome

- Central cyanosis (right-to-left shunting of deoxygenated blood): blue-purple discolouration of lips, tongue, oral mucosa. Distinguish from peripheral cyanosis.
- Clubbing: in all longstanding Eisenmenger lesions. Differential clubbing (only lower limbs) in PDA-Eisenmenger.
- Polycythaemia: compensatory erythrocytosis from chronic hypoxaemia. Haematocrit may reach 60–70%.
- Loud P2: always present in Eisenmenger — the suprasystemic PA pressure snaps the pulmonic valve shut with great force. Often palpable at the LUSB.
- Murmur: the original murmur shortens dramatically or disappears as pulmonary pressure equalises with systemic. With equal pressures: no pressure gradient → no turbulence → no murmur. The disappearance of the murmur in a previously-known VSD patient is a sign of Eisenmenger.
- Peripheral oedema, ascites, hepatomegaly: from right heart failure, which develops late in Eisenmenger. Also associated with haemoptysis (pulmonary vascular disease), paradoxical emboli (right-to-left shunting → clots/air from venous system reach the systemic circulation).

Exam tip: The S2 splitting as the master CHD clue:
• Fixed wide splitting: ASD (pathognomonic)
• Wide non-fixed splitting: RBBB, PS
• Paradoxical (reversed) splitting: LBBB, severe AS
• Single S2: TOF (absent P2), severe AS (absent A2), Eisenmenger (equal pressures)
• Loud P2: pulmonary hypertension, Eisenmenger, severe MS
Always assess S2 before attributing a murmur to a specific lesion — the S2 character often clinches the anatomy.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
The peripheral vasculature is the final common pathway of cardiovascular function — it is where the heart's output meets the tissues' demand. Peripheral arterial disease, venous insufficiency, and the acute presentations of limb ischaemia each have clinical signs that must be systematically sought in every cardiovascular patient.

## Peripheral pulse examination — systematic approach

Examine all major peripheral pulses bilaterally and simultaneously where possible: radial, brachial, carotid (one side at a time — bilateral carotid pressure → ↓ cerebral perfusion → syncope), femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis. For each: presence, volume, and character.

Pulse | Location | Technique
Radial | Lateral aspect of the wrist | Two or three fingertips over the radial styloid
Brachial | Medial aspect of the antecubital fossa | Thumb on the lateral side, fingertips pressing medially
Carotid | Medial to the SCM at the level of the thyroid cartilage | One side at a time; never both simultaneously. Use fingertips, NOT thumb (can create carotid sinus pressure effect)
Femoral | Mid-inguinal point (halfway between ASIS and pubic symphysis) | Firm pressure; in obese patients, deeper palpation required
Popliteal | Popliteal fossa behind the knee | Flex the knee to 30–45°; both hands around the knee, thumbs anteriorly, fingertips pressing into the popliteal fossa from behind
Posterior tibial | Posterior to the medial malleolus | Press fingertips into the groove behind the medial malleolus
Dorsalis pedis | Dorsum of the foot between 1st and 2nd metatarsals | Light fingertip pressure in the groove between the 1st and 2nd metatarsals

## Acute limb ischaemia — the 6 Ps

Sign: The 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia — a surgical emergency
Pain: severe, sudden, unrelenting. Early: well-localised. Late: diffuse from tissue necrosis.
Pallor: the limb appears white or ashen — no blood reaching the tissue distal to the occlusion.
Pulselessness: absent pulses distal to the occlusion (may be absent at multiple levels).
Paraesthesia: tingling, numbness — early sign of nerve ischaemia (earliest structure to be ischaemia-sensitive). If paraesthesia is present → limb viability is threatened → surgical urgency.
Paralysis: inability to move the limb — late sign indicating motor nerve and muscle ischaemia. Limb is no longer viable → emergency revascularisation.
Perishing cold: the ischaemic limb is strikingly cold compared with the contralateral side and the patient's proximal limb.
Paraesthesia and paralysis indicate the limb is immediately threatened — time to operating theatre or angiography should be minutes to <6 hours.

## Chronic limb ischaemia — signs of PAD

- Hair loss: below the level of arterial insufficiency
- Thin, shiny, atrophic skin: reduced blood flow → impaired skin nutrition
- Thickened nails: chronically ischaemic nail beds grow slowly → thickened, brittle nails
- Muscle wasting: chronically ischaemic muscles lose bulk
- Dependent rubor: the ischaemic foot becomes intensely red/purple when hanging down (vasodilated capillaries still fill by gravity); becomes pallid when elevated above heart level (insufficient arterial pressure to fill against gravity). Buerger's test: (1) elevate the leg to 45° for 2 minutes — normal stays pink; PAD → pallor appears. (2) Hang the leg over the side of the bed — normal: colour returns in <5 seconds; PAD: colour return >15 seconds + dependent rubor.
- Ulcers: arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out, with pale/grey base, occur on the tips of toes, pressure points, dorsum of foot. Venous ulcers: painless or mildly painful, irregular margins, pigmented (hemosiderin), above the medial malleolus, associated with lipodermatosclerosis.

## Allen's test — pre-radial artery cannulation

Before radial artery cannulation (arterial line, ABG, radial artery graft harvest): (1) ask the patient to make a tight fist while you compress both radial and ulnar arteries; (2) ask them to open the hand — it should be pale/white; (3) release the ulnar artery only; (4) normal: colour returns to the palm within 5–7 seconds (positive Allen's = adequate ulnar collateral). If colour does not return within 10 seconds: negative Allen's = inadequate ulnar collateral → do NOT cannulate the radial artery (risk of hand ischaemia).

sections.body:
Every examination has a consistent set of errors that candidates make — not from ignorance of facts but from overlooked technique, incomplete sequences, or failure to integrate findings. This chapter systematically documents the 30 most common errors, paired with the correction. Reviewing this chapter the night before an examination or clinical posting is the highest-yield use of 30 minutes.

## Errors in preparation and positioning

Common mistake: MISTAKE 1: Not exposing the patient adequately. Examining through clothing or with the chest incompletely exposed.

Correct approach: The entire anterior chest must be exposed. For female patients: expose the chest and cover with a gown between examination steps — this is appropriate clinical technique. The apex beat, parasternal heave, and lower cardiac border cannot be properly assessed through clothing.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 2: Starting auscultation without palpation. Going directly from pulse to stethoscope.

Correct approach: Always inspect → palpate (apex, heave, thrill) → then auscultate. Palpation findings (displaced apex = LV enlargement; parasternal heave = RV enlargement; thrill = grade ≥4 murmur) inform and focus auscultation.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 3: Not turning the patient to the left lateral decubitus position for apex beat assessment and S3/S4/MS rumble auscultation.

Correct approach: The left lateral decubitus position brings the apex closer to the chest wall — essential for: (1) accurate apex beat characterisation; (2) hearing the S3 and S4 gallops; (3) bringing out the mid-diastolic rumble of MS. Always complete this position change before concluding the cardiac examination.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 4: Not leaning the patient forward for AR murmur auscultation.

Correct approach: The early diastolic murmur of AR is best heard with the patient sitting up, leaning forward, breath held in full expiration, with the diaphragm pressed firmly at the left sternal border (3rd–4th ICS). This is the ONLY murmur that requires this specific position. Omitting it = missing a soft AR murmur.

## Errors in pulse examination

Common mistake: MISTAKE 5: Counting the pulse for 15 seconds × 4 in an irregular rhythm.

Correct approach: In any irregular rhythm (especially AF), count for a full 60 seconds. The 15-second extrapolation introduces up to 25% error in the rate estimate.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 6: Not comparing both radial pulses simultaneously.

Correct approach: Always palpate both radials simultaneously. Radio-radial delay (subclavian stenosis, aortic dissection) is only detectable when both are felt at the same time. Note this explicitly in every examination presentation.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 7: Forgetting to lift the arm to elicit a collapsing pulse.

Correct approach: At heart level, a mild or moderate collapsing pulse in AR may feel nearly normal. Ask the patient's permission, grasp the forearm, and lift it above the shoulder. The collapsing quality is dramatically amplified by the gravity effect.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 8: Not checking for radio-femoral delay.

Correct approach: In any young hypertensive patient, or when coarctation is in the differential, always check radio-femoral delay. Palpate the right radial and right femoral simultaneously — the femoral should arrive with only an imperceptibly brief delay. A clearly felt delay = coarctation until proven otherwise.

## Errors in JVP assessment

Common mistake: MISTAKE 9: Using the external jugular vein (EJV) instead of the internal jugular vein (IJV).

Correct approach: The EJV has valves and may be kinked at the entry to the subclavian vein → falsely elevated. Always assess the IJV (the undulating pulsation visible behind/between the SCM heads). If only the EJV is assessable: state this explicitly and note that the reading may overestimate the true RA pressure.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 10: Measuring the horizontal distance rather than the vertical height of the JVP from the sternal angle.

Correct approach: The JVP height is the vertical distance from the sternal angle to the top of the JVP pulsation. Use a ruler or a card held horizontally at the sternal angle and vertically at the JVP level to ensure a true right-angle measurement. Measuring the slanted distance overestimates the JVP height.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 11: Saying "hepatojugular reflux" instead of "abdominojugular reflux" (AJR).

Correct approach: The correct term is abdominojugular reflux. The test works with pressure applied anywhere on the abdomen (including above the liver). "Hepatojugular" implies the response comes specifically from the liver — it does not. More importantly, in examinations this terminology error marks a candidate as imprecise.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 12: Not performing the AJR test in a patient with suspected heart failure.

Correct approach: AJR is a sensitive marker of elevated right heart filling pressure, often positive before the JVP is overtly elevated. Always perform it. Technique: sustained 15-second firm abdominal pressure, patient breathing normally (not breath-holding — Valsalva from breath-holding gives a false-positive result).

## Errors in auscultation

Common mistake: MISTAKE 13: Using only the diaphragm — missing S3, S4, and the MS diastolic rumble.

Correct approach: The bell of the stethoscope (applied with light pressure so the skin acts as a membrane) is essential for: S3, S4, the MS diastolic rumble. The diaphragm misses these. Develop the habit of listening with both diaphragm AND bell at each auscultatory area.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 14: Not auscultating in the axilla and carotids.

Correct approach: MR murmur radiates to the left axilla — auscultate there. AS murmur radiates to the carotids bilaterally — auscultate both carotids. These radiation patterns are frequently tested and frequently omitted by candidates.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 15: Failing to distinguish fixed splitting of S2 from physiological splitting by not comparing inspiration vs expiration.

Correct approach: Ask the patient to breathe normally. Listen to S2 on inspiration and on expiration. Fixed splitting (ASD) = the gap between A2 and P2 does NOT change with respiration. Physiological splitting = gap widens on inspiration, disappears on expiration. This single observation can diagnose ASD on auscultation.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 16: Confusing the opening snap of MS with P2 (concluding the patient has a wide split S2).

Correct approach: P2 is at the LUSB and changes with respiration. The opening snap is best heard at the LLSB/apex and does not change with respiration. Additionally: the S2-OS interval is shorter than the A2-P2 interval of wide splitting; the OS is followed by the diastolic rumble. If in doubt: assess respiratory variation (OS = fixed; P2 = moves with respiration).

Common mistake: MISTAKE 17: Not performing dynamic auscultation for HOCM and MVP.

Correct approach: Any ESM that does NOT radiate to the carotids (unlike AS), or any mid-systolic click, requires dynamic auscultation: ask the patient to stand, then squat, then strain (Valsalva). HOCM: louder on standing/Valsalva, softer on squatting. MVP: click moves earlier on standing/Valsalva, later on squatting. This differentiates three diagnoses with overlapping murmur character at rest.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 18: Describing every systolic murmur as "ejection systolic" without checking if it truly starts after S1.

Correct approach: A pansystolic murmur (MR, TR, VSD) begins with S1 — there is no gap between S1 and the onset of the murmur. An ejection systolic murmur (AS, PS, HOCM, innocent) begins after S1 — there is a gap. This distinction changes the diagnosis fundamentally. Listen carefully to whether S1 is audible separately from the start of the murmur.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 19: Calling the Rivero-Carvalho sign as "inspiration increases all right-sided murmurs" without understanding the exception (pulmonary ejection click decreases on inspiration).

Correct approach: The pulmonary ejection click (in PS) is the only right-sided sound that paradoxically DECREASES (or disappears) on inspiration. All other right-sided murmurs/sounds increase. The pulmonary ejection click decreases because ↑ venous return on inspiration partially pre-opens the PV during atrial systole → the click is no longer needed at the start of RV systole. This reversal is pathognomonic of PS.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 20: Not listening for the murmur of AR with the patient in the specific "lean-forward-breath-held-expiration" position.

Correct approach: The AR murmur is the most commonly missed murmur due to position omission. A soft AR murmur (grade 1–2/6) may be inaudible in any other position. The correct position: patient sits up → leans forward → holds breath at end-expiration → firm diaphragm pressure at the 3rd–4th left ICS. If AR is suspected from the pulse character (collapsing) and wide pulse pressure, this position is mandatory.

## Errors in integration and presentation

Common mistake: MISTAKE 21: Presenting the examination findings without a summary or differential diagnosis.

Correct approach: A good clinical examination presentation ends with: "In summary, the findings suggest [primary diagnosis], with evidence of [severity/complications], consistent with [aetiology if known]." The examiner wants to see that you can synthesise individual findings into a clinical picture.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 22: Not noting the presence or absence of surgical scars before beginning.

Correct approach: A midline sternotomy scar changes the entire examination interpretation (prior cardiac surgery). Always inspect for scars before anything else. In an examination, a well-healed scar may be subtle — look carefully along the entire sternum and in the infraclavicular regions (pacemaker).

Common mistake: MISTAKE 23: Confusing the Austin Flint murmur of AR with mitral stenosis.

Correct approach: Austin Flint has no opening snap; no loud S1; the AR murmur and signs of wide pulse pressure are present. MS has an opening snap; loud S1; slow-rising pulse is absent; no collapsing pulse. The echo will always distinguish them — but on clinical examination, the Austin Flint murmur is softer, without the sharp OS, and in the context of severe AR signs.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 24: Missing differential cyanosis in PDA-Eisenmenger.

Correct approach: Always check the toenails in any patient with central cyanosis. In PDA-Eisenmenger, the right-to-left shunt enters the descending aorta below the subclavian arteries → lower limbs are cyanosed and clubbed; upper limbs (left arm may be slightly affected if left subclavian origin is near the duct) appear pink. This is diagnostic of PDA-Eisenmenger.

Common mistake: MISTAKE 25: Forgetting that an S4 gallop is IMPOSSIBLE in atrial fibrillation.

Correct approach: S4 requires organised atrial contraction (the late diastolic "kick" against a stiff ventricle). AF has no organised atrial contraction. If you hear what sounds like a four-sound complex in AF, it is a summation gallop (S3 + S4 fuse when heart rate is fast and diastole is short). Never report S4 in AF — correct it in the examination if you have already stated it.
